title: Session 8 — Mini-Project
text:
The mini-project is the compulsory group activity of the course: six groups each investigate a research question with geographic data and simulated health outcomes from Västra Götaland, and present their findings in 10 minutes. It is assessed Pass/Fail.
This page is not a solution to any project. For each group’s question it lists which concepts the question tests, which app sections explain them, and what a good interpretation must address. Because every group’s question is also a classic exam question, all six are worth reviewing, not only your own.

title: Session 8 — Mini-Project
section: 8.1 What is assessed and what to present
text:
8.1 What is assessed and what to present

In short. Apply the methods, interpret the results, communicate the findings, not reproduce R output. 4–6 slides, 10 minutes, then 20–30 seconds per person on your contribution and your key takeaway.

Slides (about 4–6):

The research question and analytical approach.
Key results, supported by about 2–3 figures or tables.
Interpretation of the findings.
Important limitations or considerations.

Focus on what the results mean, not on R code. There is no written report.
Each member at the end (about 20–30 seconds): your contribution (for example analysis, visualization, interpretation, slides) and your key takeaway (the most important thing you learned).
Assessed (Pass/Fail) on: appropriate application of the methods, correct interpretation of the results, clear communication, and active participation in the group work and discussions.






TipA limitations slide that works for every group



Simulated outcomes (results are not real VGR patterns) · choice of spatial weights · the MAUP (results depend on the area units) · the ecological fallacy (area-level, not individual-level conclusions) · association, not causation.

title: Session 6 — Additional Methods and Applications
text:
Sessions 1–4 built the core toolbox: maps and rates, spatial weights and Moran’s I, spatial regression, Bayesian disease mapping. Session 6 widens the toolbox with four perspectives, each answering a different kind of question (slide 2):
The thread through all four: from exploring spatial patterns to informing public health interventions. The session ends where Session 1 started: spatial epidemiology should describe → model → evaluate interventions.

title: Session 6 — Additional Methods and Applications
section: 6.1 Four complementary perspectives
text:
6.1 Four complementary perspectives

In short. Different questions need different methods: where and what pattern? (ESDA), can people reach care? (accessibility), how do many neighbourhood variables fit together? (PCA and clustering), and what if we intervene? (causal designs).

The four parts are not a sequence of steps that every study must go through; they are four lenses. A single project can use several. The example running through Part III (Kolak et al. 2020; Lin et al. 2022) does: it summarizes 15 neighbourhood variables with PCA, groups areas with clustering, and then uses the summaries in spatial regression.

title: Session 6 — Additional Methods and Applications
section: 6.2 ESDA: link a non-spatial view and a map
text:
6.2 ESDA: link a non-spatial view and a map

In short. ESDA puts an ordinary chart (histogram, box plot, scatter plot) next to a map and links them: select bars or points in the chart and the matching areas light up on the map, and the other way round.
Think of it as: Highlighting rows in a spreadsheet and seeing where those rows are.

Univariate ESDA (slide 4). A histogram of, say, the share of children per neighbourhood says how values are distributed but not where. Linked to a map, selecting the highest bars shows whether the high values sit together (a cluster) or are scattered. This linking (selecting in one view, highlighting in another) is the key idea; brushing is the same with a selection box that you move around the map, so the linked views update as you move.
What ESDA adds to Session 2. Moran’s I and LISA (2.11, 2.13) test for spatial dependence. ESDA tools are broader and looser: they help you see patterns, outliers and differences between regions before you decide what to model.

On the exam, be able to say: ESDA links non-spatial graphs (histogram, box plot, scatter plot) with a map, so a selection in one view highlights the same observations in the other. It is used to detect patterns and generate hypotheses, not to test causal claims.

title: Session 6 — Additional Methods and Applications
section: 6.3 Bivariate ESDA: linear and local regression fits
text:
6.3 Bivariate ESDA: linear and local regression fits

In short. A scatter plot with a straight line shows the average linear association. A local regression smoother (LOWESS) follows the data more flexibly and can reveal nonlinearity or a structural break: a point where the relationship changes.

Linear fit (slide 5). GeoDa adds the regression line and summary statistics (intercept, slope, R², p-values) to the scatter plot.
Local regression fit (slide 6). LOWESS (locally weighted scatter plot smoother) computes a slope on a small interval of the x-axis, giving less weight to points further away, and combines these local fits across the full range into a smooth curve.
Slide 6 asks: what pattern do you see? In the slide’s example the LOWESS curve is fairly flat at low x and then rises steeply at high x: the relationship is not one straight line. A single linear slope averages two different regimes. This may suggest a structural break: the process behind the data could differ between groups of observations, and if those groups are spatially defined, that is spatial heterogeneity (6.5).








Figure 1: Simulated data with a structural break at x = 40: a gentle slope below, a steep one above. The straight line (grey) averages the two regimes and fits neither well. The LOWESS curve (purple) bends at the break.






On the exam, be able to say: A linear fit gives one average slope; LOWESS fits local slopes on small intervals (nearby points weighted more) and joins them into a smooth curve. A bend in the LOWESS curve suggests nonlinearity or a structural break, which can hint at spatial heterogeneity.

title: Session 6 — Additional Methods and Applications
section: 6.4 The bandwidth controls the smoothness
text:
6.4 The bandwidth controls the smoothness

In short. The bandwidth is the share of the x-range used for each local fit. Small bandwidth → wiggly curve that chases noise; large bandwidth → smooth curve that can hide real bends.
Think of it as: Averaging over a few neighbours or over the whole street.

The bandwidth is given as a fraction of the total range in x (slide 7). There is literature and debate about the optimal bandwidth; there is no single right answer.
Slide 7 asks: which one is the result of a larger bandwidth? The smoother curve. A larger bandwidth uses more of the data for each local fit, so each local slope averages over more points and the curve changes slowly. The jagged curve comes from a small bandwidth.








Figure 2: The same simulated data smoothed with LOWESS at two bandwidths. Left: bandwidth 0.15 (each local fit uses 15% of the data) gives a jagged curve that follows noise. Right: bandwidth 0.7 gives a smooth curve. The straight line is the linear fit.






Common confusion: “the bandwidth is a number of neighbours on the map”. No: in a LOWESS scatter plot the bandwidth is about the x-axis (attribute space), not geographic distance. It decides how many observations with similar x-values enter each local fit.


On the exam, be able to say: The bandwidth is the fraction of the x-range used in each local fit. Larger bandwidth gives a smoother curve (risk: hiding real structure); smaller gives a wigglier curve (risk: fitting noise).

title: Session 6 — Additional Methods and Applications
section: 6.5 Spatial heterogeneity, revisited
text:
6.5 Spatial heterogeneity, revisited

In short. Spatial heterogeneity means different spatial processes in different places: rural and urban, east and west. It can show up as different means, medians or regression slopes between regions.

Session 1 introduced the idea (1.12): heterogeneity is about the process or relationship differing by location; dependence is about neighbours resembling each other. Slide 8 lists three forms heterogeneity can take:



Form
Example
ESDA tool




Different means (or medians)
Average income higher in the urban core than in the suburbs
Averages chart (6.6)


Different slopes
Deprivation predicts mortality strongly in rural areas, weakly in urban
Brushing the scatter plot (6.7)


Different processes in general
Different drivers of disease in different regions
Spatial regime models (6.8), Lin et al. 2022 (6.20)




On the exam, be able to say: Spatial heterogeneity is the existence of different spatial processes in spatially defined subregions (rural/urban, east/west). It can appear as different means or medians, or as different slopes in a regression.

title: Session 6 — Additional Methods and Applications
section: 6.6 Averages chart: is the mean different inside the selection?
text:
6.6 Averages chart: is the mean different inside the selection?

In short. Select a region on the map (for example the urban core), and the averages chart tests whether the mean of a variable differs between selected and unselected areas. The selection is spatial, so a significant difference is evidence of heterogeneity in means.

GeoDa’s averages chart (slides 9–10) is a difference-in-means test between two groups. With two groups the F-test it reports is equivalent to a t-test (F = t², same p-value). Combined with map brushing, you can move the selection and watch whether the difference holds up.








Figure 3: Averages chart on simulated data. Left: a 10 × 10 grid of areas with a spatially selected block (outlined, the ‘urban core’). Right: values in selected and unselected areas with their means. The t-test compares the two means; with two groups F = t².






On the exam, be able to say: The averages chart tests the difference in means between a spatially selected group of areas and the rest. With two groups the F-test equals a t-test. A difference suggests spatial heterogeneity in the mean.

title: Session 6 — Additional Methods and Applications
section: 6.7 Brushing the scatter plot: are the slopes different?
text:
6.7 Brushing the scatter plot: are the slopes different?

In short. Select areas on the map and the scatter plot shows two regression lines: one for the selected areas, one for the rest. Different slopes mean the relationship itself differs by place: heterogeneity in slopes.

On slide 11, selecting part of New York on the map splits the scatter plot into a red line (selected) and a blue line (unselected). GeoDa reports both fits and a Chow test of whether the coefficients are equal in the two subsets. A significant Chow test is evidence of a structural break between the regions.








Figure 4: Brushing the scatter plot, simulated. The same x–y relationship has a steep slope in the selected areas (orange) and a flat one in the rest (blue). A single pooled line (grey) would describe neither group.






On the exam, be able to say: Brushing the scatter plot fits separate regression lines to the selected and unselected areas. Different slopes (tested with a Chow test) indicate that the relationship varies by place: spatial heterogeneity.

title: Session 6 — Additional Methods and Applications
section: 6.8 What ESDA cannot do
text:
6.8 What ESDA cannot do

In short. ESDA is for generating hypotheses and detecting patterns, not for drawing conclusions. Its simple tests ignore spatial autocorrelation and unequal variances, and say nothing about causes.

Slide 12 lists the limits:

The tests in the averages chart and the brushed scatter plot do not account for heteroskedasticity or spatial autocorrelation. With positively autocorrelated data the effective sample size is smaller than the number of areas, so p-values are too optimistic (the same problem as OLS in 3.1).
A more advanced approach is a spatial regime regression model: separate coefficients for each region (regime), estimated jointly, optionally with SAR or SEM dependence. This is what Lin et al. (2022) do for rural, suburban and urban counties (6.20).
Exploratory means exploratory: the selection was often chosen after looking at the map, so a “significant” difference is a hypothesis to test in new data, not a finding.

Other GeoDa ESDA tools extend the same idea to many variables (multivariate) and to space–time data; see Resources.






TipWhen to use ESDA



At the start of an analysis: to understand distributions, spot outliers and data errors, see whether patterns cluster, and form hypotheses about regions where processes might differ.



On the exam, be able to say: ESDA generates hypotheses and detects patterns; it does not draw causal conclusions. Its simple tests ignore heteroskedasticity and spatial autocorrelation; spatial regime models are the more advanced alternative.

title: Session 6 — Additional Methods and Applications
section: 6.9 Access is multidimensional
text:
6.9 Access is multidimensional

In short. “Access” to care is more than distance. The classical model has five dimensions (the five A’s), and spatial distance is only one of them: geographic accessibility.

Penchansky & Thomas (1981) define access as the degree of “fit” between clients and the health care system, along five dimensions:








Dimension
Question
Example




Availability
Are there enough services for the need?
Number of GPs relative to the population


Accessibility
Can people physically reach them?
Distance, travel time, transport


Affordability
Can people pay?
Fees, insurance, lost income


Acceptability
Do people find them acceptable, and does the provider accept them?
Language, gender of staff, trust


Accommodation
Is the service organised so people can use it?
Opening hours, appointment system, walk-ins



Spatial accessibility measures mainly capture availability and accessibility, the two dimensions with a geography. A short drive to a clinic that is closed in the evenings, unaffordable or culturally unacceptable is not good access.

On the exam, be able to say: Access is the fit between clients and the system, with five dimensions: availability, accessibility, affordability, acceptability and accommodation (Penchansky & Thomas 1981). Spatial measures capture mainly availability and geographic accessibility.

title: Session 6 — Additional Methods and Applications
section: 6.10 Why the choice of accessibility measure matters
text:
6.10 Why the choice of accessibility measure matters

In short. Different access measures can lead to different conclusions about whether there is a spatial mismatch or inequity (Talen & Anselin 1998). So the measure must fit the problem.

Accessibility is also part of location optimization (slide 15), which considers:

supply and demand at the destinations (facilities) and origins (where people live);
the coverage problem: where to place facilities so that as many people as possible are within reach;
the location–allocation problem: which facility each person’s demand is assigned to.

Two questions make choosing the “right” measure complicated (slide 16):

How should the distance between patient and facility be characterized? Straight line, road network, travel time by car or by public transport?
What assumptions about travel behaviour are appropriate? Do people go to the nearest facility? Do they cross administrative borders? Do they travel from home or from work?

Talen & Anselin (1998) compared several measures of access to public playgrounds and found that which neighbourhoods looked under-served depended on the measure. The same can happen with clinics or pharmacies.

On the exam, be able to say: Different access measures can give different conclusions about spatial mismatch and inequity (Talen & Anselin 1998). The choice depends on how distance is characterized and what is assumed about travel behaviour, so the measure should match the problem.

title: Session 6 — Additional Methods and Applications
section: 6.11 Container methods: counts inside areas or buffers
text:
6.11 Container methods: counts inside areas or buffers

In short. A container measure counts facilities inside a unit: an administrative area (point-in-polygon) or a buffer around it. Simple, but it depends on where the borders are and ignores what lies just outside.
Think of it as: Counting the shops on your own postcode and ignoring the one across the street in the next postcode.









Technique
What is counted
Example (slide 18)




Point-in-polygon
Facilities inside each area
How many methadone providers are in each zip code?


Buffer analysis
Facilities near the area, as well as within it
How many providers are within a 1-mile buffer?


Buffer coverage
Share of the area covered by facility buffers
What percentage of the area is within a threshold of a provider’s service?



Slide 19’s example: an area with one provider inside it counts N = 1 with point-in-polygon; adding 1-mile buffers around providers, a provider just outside the border also reaches it, so the buffer count is N = 2.








Figure 5: Container methods, schematic. Left: point-in-polygon counts the one provider inside the area (N = 1). Right: with buffers around providers, the provider just outside the border also reaches the area (N = 2). The provider far away counts in neither.





But what about… (slide 19): the sensitivity to tract or buffer boundaries (a MAUP problem, 1.10); how certain we are that the buffer size is right (why 1 mile?); street networks (a straight-line buffer ignores rivers and roads); and other modes of transport (walking, driving, transit).
Slide 20’s advice: think about the spatial process of your phenomenon, and whether it cares about existing borders. People cross zip-code borders to get care; a container measure assumes they do not.

On the exam, be able to say: Container methods count facilities within an area (point-in-polygon) or within buffers. Limitations: results depend on boundaries and buffer size, straight-line buffers ignore networks and transport modes, and access across borders is ignored.

title: Session 6 — Additional Methods and Applications
section: 6.12 Proximity methods: minimum distance, travel cost, gravity
text:
6.12 Proximity methods: minimum distance, travel cost, gravity

In short. Proximity measures use distance or travel time instead of borders: distance to the nearest facility, the average distance to all, or a gravity score where big, close facilities count most.










Measure
Definition (slide 21)
Captures
Ignores




Minimum distance
Distance from the origin to the nearest destination
How far the closest option is
How many options; whether the nearest is overloaded


Travel cost
Total or average distance (or travel time) between the origin and the destinations
Overall remoteness
Size and capacity of facilities


Travel time
Minutes along the network by a given mode
Realistic travel burden
Depends on mode; data hungry


Gravity potential
Resources weighted by size and adjusted for the “friction of distance”
Several facilities, their size, and decay with distance
Competition between people for the same facility



A common form of the gravity potential (not on the slides) is
\[
A_i = \sum_j \frac{S_j}{d_{ij}^{\,\beta}}
\]

In words: the accessibility of place i adds up every facility j’s size Sⱼ (for example number of doctors), discounted by the distance dᵢⱼ to the power β. Large, close facilities contribute most; β sets how fast the pull fades with distance.

Slide 17 maps four measures for the same state side by side (time to nearest resource, number within 30 minutes, an access score, minimum distance): the maps do not look the same, which is the point of 6.10.

On the exam, be able to say: Minimum distance = distance to the nearest facility; travel cost = total or average distance to facilities; gravity potential = facility size weighted by a distance-decay function. Proximity measures avoid border problems but, except gravity, ignore facility size, and none of them handles competition (demand).

title: Session 6 — Additional Methods and Applications
section: 6.13 Floating catchment area (2SFCA) models: supply and demand
text:
6.13 Floating catchment area (2SFCA) models: supply and demand

In short. Floating catchment area (FCA) methods take both supply and demand into account: a clinic with 10 doctors serving 30,000 people offers less per person than one serving 5,000. The two-step version (2SFCA) computes a provider-to-population ratio for each facility and then adds up the ratios each place can reach.

FCA models address the limitations of the simpler measures (slide 22):

Distance-based measures cannot incorporate differences in availability between facilities (size, capacity, how many people compete for them).
Container-based measures ignore distance within the container and the possibility of using services outside it.

The two steps (the standard 2SFCA; the formulas are not on the slides, see Bryant & Delamater 2019 and Luo & Qi 2009 on Resources):

For each facility j: find all population locations within its catchment (for example 30 minutes), and compute the supply-to-demand ratio Rⱼ = Sⱼ / Σ Pₖ (doctors per person in reach).
For each population location i: add up the ratios Rⱼ of all facilities within the catchment of i. Aᵢ = Σ Rⱼ.


Worked example (made-up numbers). Two clinics, three neighbourhoods. Clinic F1 has 10 doctors and reaches neighbourhoods 1 and 2; clinic F2 has 4 doctors and reaches neighbourhoods 2 and 3.




Population
Clinics in reach




Neighbourhood 1
20,000
F1


Neighbourhood 2
10,000
F1, F2


Neighbourhood 3
15,000
F2



Step 1. R₁ = 10 / (20,000 + 10,000) = 0.333 per 1,000; R₂ = 4 / (10,000 + 15,000) = 0.160 per 1,000.
Step 2. A₁ = 0.333; A₂ = 0.333 + 0.160 = 0.493; A₃ = 0.160 doctors per 1,000 residents.
If F1 lies inside neighbourhood 1 and F2 inside neighbourhood 3, a point-in-polygon count gives neighbourhood 2 zero clinics, yet by 2SFCA it has the best access, because it can reach both.










NoteDeeper: FCA extensions (slide 23)





The basic 2SFCA treats everyone inside the catchment as equally close and everyone outside as unable to reach. Extensions relax this:

Enhanced 2SFCA (E2SFCA), Luo & Qi (2009): distance-decay weights within sub-zones of the catchment.
Kernel density 2SFCA (KD2SFCA), Dai & Wang (2011): a continuous kernel distance-decay function.
Modified 2SFCA (M2SFCA), Delamater (2013): accounts for suboptimal configuration (facilities placed far from people).
Three-step FCA (3SFCA), Wan, Zou & Sternberg (2012): adds a selection weight for competition between nearby facilities.
Rational agent access model (RAAM), Saxon & Snow (2019): people choose facilities by balancing travel time and congestion.










WarningLimitations



The catchment size and distance-decay function are choices that change the results. FCA still measures potential spatial access (availability + accessibility), not affordability, acceptability or accommodation (6.9), and not whether people actually use the services.



On the exam, be able to say: 2SFCA: (1) for each facility, supply divided by the population within its catchment; (2) for each location, the sum of these ratios over facilities in reach. It combines supply, demand and distance, unlike container measures (borders) and minimum distance (no capacity or competition).

title: Session 6 — Additional Methods and Applications
section: 6.15 Why reduce dimensions? The curse of dimensionality
text:
6.15 Why reduce dimensions? The curse of dimensionality

In short. With many variables, data become sparse: methods that work in a few dimensions break down. Many neighbourhood indicators are also highly correlated, so they repeat the same information. Dimension reduction summarizes them in a few new variables.

The curse of dimensionality (Bellman 1961): methods that work in a small number of dimensions may not work in high-dimensional spaces (many variables or features). Problems include (slide 25):

Increased sparsity. Imagine 10 points on a line, then in a square, then in a cube: the same 10 points fill less and less of the space. To keep the same density in 3 dimensions you need 10³ = 1,000 points.
More data needed to keep the same accuracy.
Computational complexity.

In spatial epidemiology: social determinants of health (SDOH) are measured by many indicators (poverty, education, unemployment, crowding, car ownership …) for each area. Putting all of them in one regression gives unstable, hard-to-interpret coefficients because they are collinear. One solution: principal components analysis.

On the exam, be able to say: The curse of dimensionality: with many variables data become sparse, more data are needed and computation grows; methods that work in few dimensions may fail. Correlated neighbourhood indicators can be summarized with PCA.

title: Session 6 — Additional Methods and Applications
section: 6.16 Principal components analysis (PCA)

title: Session 6 — Additional Methods and Applications
section: 6.17 Example: an SDOH index from 15 variables (Kolak et al. 2020)
text:
6.17 Example: an SDOH index from 15 variables (Kolak et al. 2020)

In short. Kolak et al. reduced 15 neighbourhood indicators of social determinants of health in US census tracts to 4 components that keep 71% of the variance, then named and mapped them.

Input (slide 27). Fifteen variables chosen to capture small-area variation in economic status, social and neighbourhood characteristics, housing and transportation, and demographic characteristics of vulnerable groups; stratified across social, economic and physical environments. Many are highly correlated (poverty, income, unemployment, education …).
Output (slide 28). Four orthogonal components, interpreted as indices:







SDOH index
Captures




Socioeconomic advantage index (SES)
Poverty and education level; strongly correlated with an area deprivation index


Limited mobility index (MOB)
Share of older adults and persons with disabilities


Urban core opportunity index (URB)
Highly urbanized populations with more opportunities and high living costs


Mixed immigrant cohesion and accessibility index (MICA)
Immigrant populations with traditional family structures and multiple accessibility stressors



Mapping (slide 29). Each index is mapped with a standard deviation map (2.2): classes in standard deviations above and below the mean, which suits a standardized component score.
After PCA you can (slide 30): interpret the index, spatialize it (map it), and cluster it using LISA (2.13) to find hot and cold spots of, for example, socioeconomic disadvantage.

On the exam, be able to say: Kolak et al. (2020) used PCA to reduce 15 correlated SDOH variables to 4 orthogonal indices (SES, MOB, URB, MICA) explaining 71% of the variance. The indices can be interpreted, mapped (standard deviation maps) and clustered with LISA.

title: Session 6 — Additional Methods and Applications
section: 6.18 Cluster analysis and K-means
text:
6.18 Cluster analysis and K-means

In short. Clustering groups areas so that similar areas end up together: high similarity within clusters, low similarity between them. K-means puts each area in exactly one of K clusters, using squared Euclidean distance, and moves areas between clusters until the within-cluster spread is smallest.

Cluster analysis (slide 31). Goal: group n observations into k clusters so that intra-cluster similarity is maximized and between-cluster similarity is minimized. It is unsupervised learning: there is no outcome variable. Many methods exist: hierarchical, density-based, grid-based, model-based …
K-means (slide 32):

Exact clustering: every observation belongs to one cluster, and only one.
Dissimilarity is the squared Euclidean distance:

\[
d_{ij}^2 = \sum_{v=1}^{p} (x_{iv} - x_{jv})^2
\]

In words: for areas i and j, take the difference on every variable v (p variables in all), square it, and add up. Large when the areas differ on many variables.


Iterative relocation minimizes the dissimilarity within clusters: start with K centres, assign each area to its nearest centre, recompute the centres as cluster means, reassign, and repeat until nothing changes.





On the exam, be able to say: Cluster analysis is unsupervised: it groups observations to maximize similarity within and minimize similarity between clusters. K-means is exact (each observation in one cluster), uses squared Euclidean distance, and iteratively relocates observations to minimize within-cluster dissimilarity.

title: Session 6 — Additional Methods and Applications
section: 6.19 How many clusters? The elbow plot
text:
6.19 How many clusters? The elbow plot

In short. The within-cluster sum of squares (WCSS) always falls as K grows (with K = n it is zero), so you cannot just minimize it. Plot WCSS against K and look for the elbow: the point after which adding clusters helps much less.









Figure 8: Elbow plot for simulated areas that truly form four groups. The within-cluster sum of squares drops steeply up to K = 4 and slowly after: the kink suggests K = 4.





Within-cluster sum of squares: smaller is better for a given K. The kink is where WCSS starts to decrease at a much slower rate (slide 34). The elbow is a heuristic: in real data it can be unclear, and interpretability of the clusters also matters. Kolak et al. ended with seven neighbourhood types.

On the exam, be able to say: WCSS always decreases with K, so choose K at the elbow of the WCSS-versus-K plot, where adding clusters stops reducing WCSS much. It is a heuristic; interpretability also matters.

title: Session 6 — Additional Methods and Applications
section: 6.20 Spatial clustering and the full workflow (PCA → clusters → spatial regression)
text:
6.20 Spatial clustering and the full workflow (PCA → clusters → spatial regression)

In short. Ordinary K-means ignores location, so one “cluster” can be scattered over the whole country. Spatial clustering also rewards closeness on the map, giving compact neighbourhood types. In a full study the PCA indices are then used as predictors in spatial regression.

Adding the spatial aspect (slide 33). Consider both attribute similarity and locational similarity. Two ways:

Add the coordinates of each area (for example the centroid of each census tract) as extra variables in K-means.
Multi-objective optimization: weight the objective of attribute similarity against the objective of geographic co-location.









Figure 9: K-means with K = 3 on simulated areas (a 12 × 12 grid) with two noisy attributes that vary smoothly across the region. Left: attributes only; clusters are fragmented, with isolated cells far from the rest of their cluster. Right: attributes plus standardized centroid coordinates as extra variables; clusters become compact regions.





Back to Kolak et al. (slides 35–36). The 4 PCA indices plus the census tract centroids went into K-means: seven clusters, a neighbourhood typology for the whole continental US (for example rural affordable, suburban affluent, urban core).
The full workflow (slide 37):





flowchart LR
  A["1 · Gather many SDOH<br/>variables, guided by<br/>a theoretical framework"] --> B["2 · PCA<br/>a few orthogonal<br/>indices"]
  B --> C["3 · Cluster analysis<br/>neighbourhood<br/>typologies"]
  B --> D["4 · Spatial regression<br/>indices → health outcome"]
  D --> E["SAR / SEM<br/>for dependence"]
  D --> F["Spatial regime model<br/>for heterogeneity"]


 Workflow: each arrow means “then”. Not causal. PCA followed by cluster analysis and spatial regression (slide 37). 



Lin et al. (2022), slide 38. The four indices were used in a spatial error model of COVID-19 mortality, estimated separately for rural, suburban and urban counties (a spatial regime model). Reading the table:

SEM handles spatial dependence: the virus is highly transmissible, so neighbouring counties’ errors are correlated.
Regimes handle spatial heterogeneity: the virus spread unevenly across places and populations.
The same index has different associations in different regimes. The socioeconomic advantage index: −1.88 (p = 0.56) in rural, −21.60 (p < 0.001) in suburban, −4.24 (p = 0.13) in urban counties. The Chow test (23.10, p < 0.001) rejects equal coefficients across the regimes.


On the exam, be able to say: Spatial clustering adds locational similarity, either by including centroid coordinates as extra variables or by weighting attribute and geographic objectives. Typical workflow: SDOH variables → PCA indices → clusters (typologies) → spatial regression with SAR/SEM for dependence and regimes for heterogeneity.

title: Session 6 — Additional Methods and Applications
section: Part IV · From spatial association to causal questions
text: Part IV · From spatial association to causal questions

title: Session 6 — Additional Methods and Applications
section: 6.21 Describe, associate, intervene
text:
6.21 Describe, associate, intervene

In short. “Areas with better healthcare access have lower mortality” is an association. Whether improving access would reduce mortality is a causal question, and needs more than a spatial model.

Slide 39 uses one statement to separate three kinds of question:








Describe
Associate
Intervene




Where are risks and services located?
How do spatial characteristics relate to health?
Would improving access actually reduce mortality?


ESDA, disease maps
Spatial regression
Causal designs



A spatial association is not, by itself, a causal effect. Areas with good access may also be richer, more urban and healthier for many other reasons. This echoes Session 1’s call to move from description to intervention (1.7) and Session 4’s warning that a high-risk area is not a causal explanation (4.22).

On the exam, be able to say: Describe (where?), associate (how is it related?) and intervene (what if we change it?) are different questions. A spatial association, even from a spatial regression, is not by itself a causal effect.

title: Session 6 — Additional Methods and Applications
section: 6.22 Three distinct challenges: dependence, confounding, interference
text:
6.22 Three distinct challenges: dependence, confounding, interference

In short. Spatial data raise three different problems for causal questions: outcomes of neighbours are correlated (dependence), geography can drive both exposure and outcome (spatially structured confounding), and an intervention in one area can change outcomes in another (interference).









Challenge
What it is (slide 40)
Example




Spatial dependence
Nearby outcomes or errors are correlated
Neighbouring areas have similar mortality rates


Spatially structured confounding
Geographic factors influence both exposure and outcome
Deprivation affects both access to care and health


Spatial interference
An intervention in one area changes outcomes in another
Residents cross municipal borders to use a new clinic











Figure 10: Causal diagram: each arrow means “directly affects”. Left: spatially structured confounding, where deprivation (a geographic factor) affects both access and health, so access and health are associated even without a causal effect. Right: interference, where the treatment of area A affects the outcome in neighbouring area B.





Spatial dependence ≠ spatial interference (slide 40). Dependence is a statement about correlated outcomes or errors; it can arise from shared unmeasured causes with no intervention at all. Interference is a causal statement: treating one unit changes another unit’s outcome. A SAR or SEM model handles dependence; it does not by itself identify interference.

On the exam, be able to say: Spatial dependence: nearby outcomes or errors are correlated. Spatially structured confounding: geographic factors affect both exposure and outcome. Spatial interference: treatment in one area changes outcomes in another. Dependence is not the same as interference.

title: Session 6 — Additional Methods and Applications
section: 6.23 Spatially structured confounding in practice
text:
6.23 Spatially structured confounding in practice

In short. Interventions are rarely placed at random: a new clinic goes where need, resources or political will are. Whatever drove the placement may also drive health, so treated and untreated areas differ before the intervention starts.

Slide 46 lists confounding as the first practical caution: policy placement may follow local need, resources, or changing health trends.

Need: screening vans are sent to areas with low participation → treated areas start out worse.
Resources: richer municipalities adopt new programmes first → treated areas start out better.
Changing trends: a programme is launched where mortality is already rising (or falling) → before–after comparisons confuse the trend with the effect.

Because these factors are spatially patterned (deprivation clusters), the confounding is spatially structured. Adding a spatial random effect or a SAR term does not automatically remove it, and can even change the exposure coefficient in unexpected ways when the exposure itself is spatially smooth. That is why Part IV turns to study design (6.25).

On the exam, be able to say: Interventions are placed according to need, resources or trends, which also affect health and are spatially patterned. This spatially structured confounding means treated and untreated areas are not comparable; study design, not only a spatial model, is needed.

title: Session 6 — Additional Methods and Applications
section: 6.24 Does a spatial lag represent a causal spillover?
text:
6.24 Does a spatial lag represent a causal spillover?

In short. Not automatically. In a SAR model, a change in x “spreads” through (I − ρW)⁻¹: that is a model-implied indirect effect. A causal spillover asks what would happen in area i if we intervened in area j, and that needs a credible design and assumptions.

The SAR model from Session 3:
\[
Y = \rho W Y + X\beta + \varepsilon
\]



Model-implied indirect effect
Causal spillover effect




In a SAR model, changes propagate through (I − ρW)⁻¹ (3.5)
How would an intervention in area j change the outcome in area i?


A property of the fitted model and the chosen W
A property of the real world


Follows from the model’s assumptions
Needs identification: a design that rules out confounding



Slide 41 asks: does a spatial lag represent a causal spillover? The indirect impacts computed from a SAR model are what the model implies if it is correct. They become a causal spillover estimate only if the model is causally right: the right W, no spatially structured confounding, the dependence really runs through the outcomes and not through omitted variables (the SEM story, 3.8). The data alone cannot establish this. A causal interpretation needs a credible design and assumptions.

On the exam, be able to say: No, not by itself. SAR indirect impacts are model-implied (they follow from (I − ρW)⁻¹ and the chosen W). A causal spillover is what an intervention in area j would do to area i, and estimating it needs a credible design and assumptions.

title: Session 6 — Additional Methods and Applications
section: 6.25 Causal designs with geographical data
text:
6.25 Causal designs with geographical data

In short. Four established designs: matching (compare similar areas), difference-in-differences (compare changes over time), geographic regression discontinuity (compare places just on either side of a border), and instrumental variables (use variation in exposure that is as good as random).




Design (slide 42)
Idea
Key assumption
Spatial twist




Matching
Compare areas with similar measured characteristics
No unmeasured confounding
Matched areas may be far apart and differ in unmeasured local context; or close together and exposed to spillover


Difference-in-differences (DiD)
Compare changes over time in treated and control areas
Parallel trends (6.26)
Neighbouring controls may be exposed (6.27)


Geographic regression discontinuity (RDD)
Compare locations close to opposite sides of a policy boundary
Nothing else changes sharply at the border
People may move or cross the border; other policies may share the same border


Instrumental variables (IV)
Use plausibly exogenous variation in exposure or treatment (for example distance to a facility)
The instrument affects the outcome only through the exposure
Distance often correlates with urbanicity and deprivation, which threatens the assumption



Geography can help design comparisons, and it introduces new threats (slide 42). A border creates a natural experiment (RDD); the same border can also be crossed (interference).

On the exam, be able to say: Matching (similar measured characteristics), difference-in-differences (changes over time, parallel trends), geographic regression discontinuity (locations close to opposite sides of a policy boundary), instrumental variables (plausibly exogenous variation in exposure). Geography helps design comparisons but adds threats such as spillovers.

title: Session 6 — Additional Methods and Applications
section: 6.26 Difference-in-differences and parallel trends
text:
6.26 Difference-in-differences and parallel trends

In short. Compare the change in the treated area with the change in a control area. Differencing removes fixed differences between the areas and shocks common to both. The key assumption: without the intervention, both would have followed parallel trends.

\[
\text{Effect} = (\text{Treated}_{\text{post}} - \text{Treated}_{\text{pre}}) - (\text{Control}_{\text{post}} - \text{Control}_{\text{pre}})
\]

In words: how much the treated area changed, minus how much it would have changed anyway, where “anyway” is borrowed from the control area’s change.










Idea
Key assumption




Slide 43
Remove time-invariant differences (one area is always poorer) and common time shocks (a national trend, a pandemic year)
Without intervention, treated and control groups would have followed parallel trends



Parallel trends concerns untreated counterfactual changes, not equal baseline levels (slide 43). The treated area may start at a much higher mortality; that is fine. What must hold is that its change without the intervention would have equalled the control’s change.








Figure 11: Difference-in-differences with made-up numbers. The treated area starts higher than the control (different levels are allowed). The dashed line is the counterfactual: the treated area’s path had it followed the control’s trend. The effect is the gap between the observed and counterfactual post values: (42 − 50) − (37 − 40) = −5.









Common confusion: “DiD needs treated and control areas with the same mortality before the intervention.” No: DiD needs parallel trends (the same change without treatment), not equal levels. Equal pre-period levels are neither necessary nor sufficient.


On the exam, be able to say: DiD effect = (treated post − treated pre) − (control post − control pre). It removes time-invariant differences and common shocks. Key assumption: parallel trends in the untreated counterfactual changes, not equal baseline levels.

title: Session 6 — Additional Methods and Applications
section: 6.27 Can a neighbouring municipality serve as a control?
text:
6.27 Can a neighbouring municipality serve as a control?

In short. Often not safely. If residents of neighbour B benefit from A’s intervention (they use A’s new clinic), B is partly treated, and using it as a control biases the DiD, usually toward zero.

Slide 44 sets up three municipalities:








A · Treated
B · Neighbour
C · Distant




Intervention introduced
Untreated, possibly exposed
Untreated, plausibly unexposed



If B benefits from A’s intervention (A → B), using B as a control may bias DiD.

Worked example (made-up numbers, deaths per 100,000). True effect of the intervention in A: −5. A: 50 → 42. Distant C: 40 → 37 (common trend −3). Neighbour B would also have followed −3, but because some residents use A’s programme it falls by an extra 2: 45 → 40.

DiD with C as control: (42 − 50) − (37 − 40) = −8 + 3 = −5 ✔
DiD with B as control: (42 − 50) − (40 − 45) = −8 + 5 = −3: the effect is underestimated, because part of the benefit shows up in the control too.


The trade-off (slide 46, spillovers): nearby controls may be exposed; distant controls may be less comparable. C is unexposed but may differ in trends (another region, another labour market). Designs that handle this explicitly define a spatial exposure for each area (6.28) or use a buffer: exclude areas close to the treated ones from the control group.

On the exam, be able to say: A neighbouring municipality may be exposed to the intervention through spillover (residents cross borders). Then it is not a clean control and DiD is biased, typically toward zero. Nearby controls risk exposure; distant controls risk being less comparable.

title: Session 6 — Additional Methods and Applications
section: 6.28 Exposure lags (WD) versus outcome lags (WY)
text:
6.28 Exposure lags (WD) versus outcome lags (WY)

In short. WY (Session 3) averages the neighbours’ outcomes. WD averages the neighbours’ treatment: how much intervention is going on around an area. They are different concepts, and defining WD still does not make an estimate causal.

A spatial treatment exposure for area i (slide 45):
\[
G_i = \sum_j w_{ij} D_j
\]

In words: Dⱼ = 1 if area j is treated, 0 if not; with row-standardized weights, Gᵢ is the share of i’s neighbours that are treated.




WY · neighbouring outcomes
WD · neighbouring treatment




A spatial lag in an outcome model: describes relationships among outcomes
An exposure measure: summarizes treatment assigned to nearby areas


Used in SAR (3.3)
Used to define who is “exposed” to spillover, for example to choose controls with Gᵢ = 0 or to estimate a spillover effect




Worked example. Area B has four neighbours (row-standardized weights 0.25 each); one of them, A, is treated. G_B = 0.25·1 + 0.25·0 + 0.25·0 + 0.25·0 = 0.25. Distant area C has no treated neighbours: G_C = 0.

Defining exposure is not enough: causal interpretation still needs identification (slide 45). The W used for G must match the real exposure pathway (where people actually travel), and the usual assumptions (no confounding, parallel trends …) still apply.

On the exam, be able to say: WY is the spatial lag of the outcome (neighbours’ outcomes, used in SAR). WD, Gᵢ = Σⱼ wᵢⱼDⱼ, is a spatial treatment exposure: the weighted share of treated neighbours. Defining exposure is not enough for causal interpretation; identification is still needed.

title: Session 6 — Additional Methods and Applications
section: 6.29 Why geography complicates causal interpretation, and choosing a method
text:
6.29 Why geography complicates causal interpretation, and choosing a method

In short. Three cautions: confounding (placement follows need), boundaries and scale (borders and W may not match real exposure), and spillovers (controls may be exposed). And one rule: choose the method that matches the question.

Practical caution (slide 46):



Confounding
Boundaries and scale
Spillovers




Policy placement may follow local need, resources or changing health trends
Administrative borders and spatial weights may not match real exposure pathways (the MAUP again, 1.10)
Nearby controls may be exposed; distant controls may be less comparable



Spatial modelling helps with dependence; study design supports causality.
Wrap-up: choose methods to match the research question (slide 47):








Where?
Associated with what?
What if we intervene?




ESDA, LISA, Bayesian disease mapping
Spatial regression and econometrics
Matching, DiD, geographic RDD, IV


Describe spatial patterns, estimate risks and quantify uncertainty
Model relationships and dependence
Identify effects under assumptions



Spatial epidemiology: describe → model → evaluate interventions.

  A Bayesian disease map of hospitalization rates for 2024
  A spatial lag model of hospitalization on distance to care
  Difference-in-differences with carefully chosen control areas
  K-means clustering of areas on deprivation indicators
  The question is “what happened because we intervened?”, so it needs a causal design. DiD compares the change in areas that got a centre with the change in comparable areas that did not, under parallel trends; controls should be chosen so that they are not exposed to the new centres. The other methods describe patterns or associations.


On the exam, be able to say: Where? → ESDA, LISA, Bayesian disease mapping. Associated with what? → spatial regression. What if we intervene? → matching, DiD, geographic RDD, IV. Spatial models help with dependence; study design supports causality, with cautions about confounding, borders and scale, and spillovers.

title: Session 6 — Additional Methods and Applications
section: 6.30 Take-home messages and key questions
text:
6.30 Take-home messages and key questions

ESDA links maps and graphs to find patterns and heterogeneity; it generates hypotheses, it does not test causes.
Access has five dimensions; spatial measures (container, proximity, gravity, 2SFCA) can disagree, so match the measure to the problem.
PCA turns many correlated SDOH indicators into a few orthogonal indices; clustering groups areas into typologies; adding location gives compact spatial clusters.
Association is not causation: separate dependence, spatially structured confounding and interference, and use a design (DiD, RDD, IV, matching) for causal questions.







NoteWhy might a container measure and a 2SFCA measure disagree about which areas are under-served?





A container measure counts facilities inside the area’s borders, ignoring both distance to facilities just outside and how many people share each facility. 2SFCA uses a catchment that crosses borders and divides supply by the population in reach. An area with no clinic inside but two nearby (zero by container) can have good 2SFCA access; a dense city area with a clinic inside can have poor 2SFCA access because many people compete for it.









NoteWhy is PCA especially useful when the SDOH variables are highly correlated?





Correlated variables share a common direction of variation. PCA puts that shared direction into one component, so a few components keep most of the variance (Kolak et al.: 4 components, 71% of 15 variables). If the variables were uncorrelated, each component would carry about the same small share and little would be gained.









NoteA SAR model shows large indirect impacts of clinic density on mortality. Can you conclude that opening a clinic in one municipality reduces mortality in its neighbours?





No. The indirect impacts are model-implied: they follow from the SAR structure and the chosen W. They would equal a causal spillover only if the model were causally correct (right W, no spatially structured confounding, the dependence really running through outcomes). A causal claim needs a design such as DiD with an exposure definition, and assumptions that can be defended.









NoteWhat is the difference between spatial dependence and spatial interference?





Spatial dependence: outcomes or errors in nearby areas are correlated, for whatever reason (shared environment, contagion, omitted variables). Spatial interference: the treatment of one area causally changes the outcome in another. Dependence can exist without any intervention; interference is about the effect of an intervention crossing borders.

title: Session 4 — Introduction to Bayesian Disease Mapping
text:
Sessions 2 and 3 described and modelled spatial dependence. Session 4 shifts the focus to estimating the underlying disease risk in each area, especially when counts are small and crude rates are unstable.
The key question on slide 3: when does a map reflect risk, and when does it reflect noise? Two areas with the same SMR of 3.0 can carry very different amounts of information (3 observed vs 1 expected, or 300 vs 100).
The answer is a Bayesian hierarchical model that lets areas borrow strength: from all areas (partial pooling, unstructured effects) and from their neighbours (spatial smoothing, structured effects). The BYM and BYM2 models combine the two. The output is not only a smoother map but a posterior distribution for every area’s relative risk, which gives credible intervals and exceedance probabilities.

title: Session 4 — Introduction to Bayesian Disease Mapping
section: 4.1 Same SMR, very different information
text:
4.1 Same SMR, very different information

In short. An SMR of 3 based on 3 cases is mostly noise; based on 300 cases it is solid. The ratio hides how much data lies behind it.
Think of it as: Three heads in three coin flips says little about the coin; 300 heads in 400 flips says a lot.





Area A
Area B




Observed Y
3
300


Expected E
1
100


SMR = Y/E
3.0
3.0


Uncertainty
Wide
Much narrower



Key question 1: why might two areas with the same SMR provide very different amounts of information? Because the information depends on the size of the counts, not the ratio. With Y ~ Poisson(Eθ), the standard error of the SMR is roughly √Y / E = SMR/√Y. Area A: 3/√3 ≈ 1.7; area B: 3/√300 ≈ 0.17, ten times smaller. One or two extra cases in A would change its SMR enormously; in B they hardly matter.
A sensible model should let the data-rich area speak more strongly than the data-poor one.





Likelihood for the relative risk θ (scaled to a maximum of 1) in two areas with the same SMR = 3. Area A (3 observed, 1 expected) is compatible with almost anything from 1 to 8; area B (300 observed, 100 expected) pins θ down near 3.





On the exam, be able to say: Same SMR, different information: the uncertainty depends on the size of the counts (SE ≈ SMR/√Y). Area A (3/1) is compatible with a wide range of risks; area B (300/100) is not.
crumbs: Session 4 — Introduction to Bayesian Disease Mapping

title: Session 4 — Introduction to Bayesian Disease Mapping
section: 4.2 Start with the estimand: which likelihood?
text:
4.2 Start with the estimand: which likelihood?

In short. Choose the model from the data: people with or without a condition out of N examined → Binomial; new events over time → Poisson with person-time; observed vs expected → Poisson with E.

First ask what is observed, what the denominator or reference is, and what quantity you want to estimate.









Outcome
Data
Likelihood
Target




Incidence / mortality
New events or deaths over population or person-time PTᵢ
Yᵢ ~ Poisson(PTᵢ λᵢ), i.e. log μᵢ = log PTᵢ + ηᵢ
Rate λᵢ


Prevalence
Existing cases among Nᵢ individuals examined
Yᵢ ~ Binomial(Nᵢ, pᵢ), logit(pᵢ) = ηᵢ
Probability pᵢ


Disease mapping with expected counts
Observed cases compared with an expected count Eᵢ
Yᵢ ~ Poisson(Eᵢ θᵢ)
Relative risk θᵢ



ηᵢ is the linear predictor on the log (or logit) scale: possibly covariates plus spatial effects.
For incidence, the offset log PTᵢ fixes the amount of exposure; the model estimates the rate.
Poisson or Binomial? Both outcomes are counts. The data structure decides the likelihood:









Binomial
Poisson




Structure
Cases among a fixed number N of individuals, each yes/no
Events over exposure or person-time


Example (slide 8)
20 people with obesity out of 100 examined
15 deaths over 10,000 person-years


Target
Probability / prevalence pᵢ
Incidence or mortality rate λᵢ



A count of cases is not automatically Poisson. And BYM/BYM2 is a spatial random-effect structure, not intrinsically a Poisson model: it can be added to the linear predictor of either.




On the exam, be able to say: Incidence: Poisson(PTᵢλᵢ), target rate. Prevalence: Binomial(Nᵢ, pᵢ), target probability. Disease mapping: Poisson(Eᵢθᵢ), target relative risk. A count is not automatically Poisson; BYM2 can be used with either.

title: Session 4 — Introduction to Bayesian Disease Mapping
section: 4.3 Observed and expected counts; indirect standardization
text:
4.3 Observed and expected counts; indirect standardization

In short. The expected count is the number of cases the area would have if its people had the reference rates (by age and sex). Comparing observed with expected removes differences in age structure.

The classical disease-mapping model:
\[
Y_i \sim \text{Poisson}(E_i\,\theta_i)
\]

In words: the observed count is random around expected count × relative risk; θᵢ is what we want to know.








Symbol
Meaning




Yᵢ
Observed number of cases or deaths in area i


Eᵢ
Expected cases if area i had the reference rates


θᵢ
Relative risk: θᵢ = 1 as expected; θᵢ > 1 elevated; θᵢ < 1 lower



The inferential target is the latent area-specific risk θᵢ.
Same model, two notations:







Disease-mapping notation
Regression notation




Yᵢ ~ Poisson(Eᵢ θᵢ), μᵢ = Eᵢ θᵢ
Yᵢ ~ Poisson(μᵢ), log μᵢ = log Eᵢ + ηᵢ, with ηᵢ = log θᵢ



log Eᵢ is the offset.
Where Eᵢ comes from: indirect standardization.
\[
E_i = \sum_a n_{ia}\, r^*_a
\]
nᵢₐ is the population of area i in stratum a (for example age × sex) and r*ₐ the reference rate in that stratum. Eᵢ is the number of cases expected from the area’s own population composition. This lets you compare areas with different age structures: an area with many elderly residents is not flagged just for being old.




On the exam, be able to say: Eᵢ = Σₐ nᵢₐ r*ₐ (indirect standardization). Yᵢ ~ Poisson(Eᵢθᵢ) is a Poisson regression with offset log Eᵢ and log θᵢ as linear predictor.

title: Session 4 — Introduction to Bayesian Disease Mapping
section: 4.4 The SMR as the crude estimate
text:
4.4 The SMR as the crude estimate

In short. The SMR is the crude, unsmoothed estimate of the relative risk: simple, but unstable when E is small.

\[
\text{SMR}_i = Y_i / E_i
\]
If each θᵢ is estimated separately, with no smoothing, the estimate is essentially the SMR (the maximum likelihood estimate of θᵢ under the Poisson model).







Strength
Problem




Simple, transparent, easy to map
Small denominators can produce extreme, unstable estimates



Extreme ≠ necessarily high underlying risk. An area with E = 0.5 and Y = 2 has SMR = 4, and with Y = 0 has SMR = 0, both from essentially no information. The variance of the SMR is roughly θᵢ/Eᵢ: the smaller Eᵢ, the noisier.

On the exam, be able to say: SMRᵢ = Yᵢ/Eᵢ, the estimate of θᵢ without smoothing. Simple and transparent, but extreme values from small denominators need not mean high risk.
crumbs: Session 4 — Introduction to Bayesian Disease Mapping

title: Session 4 — Introduction to Bayesian Disease Mapping
section: 4.5 One Bayesian idea: combine data with a model for plausible risks
text:
4.5 One Bayesian idea: combine data with a model for plausible risks

In short. Bayesian disease mapping combines what each area’s data say with a model of how areas relate, giving an updated estimate with uncertainty.

\[
\text{posterior} \;\propto\; \text{likelihood} \times \text{prior}
\]







Part
Role in disease mapping




Likelihood
What the observed counts say about each area’s risk


Prior / latent model
How areas are allowed to share information about their underlying risks


Posterior
Updated uncertainty about each area’s underlying risk



The key modelling decision: how should information be shared across areas? Not at all (SMR), with all areas equally (unstructured), or more with neighbours (spatial).

On the exam, be able to say: Posterior ∝ likelihood × prior. The key modelling decision is how areas share information.

4.6 Partial pooling and shrinkage

In short. Partial pooling: each area’s estimate is a compromise between its own data and the common pattern. Little data → pulled more (shrinkage).
Think of it as: Restaurant ratings again: few reviews → trust the typical rating more; many reviews → trust the restaurant’s own rating.

Extreme, noisy estimates move toward the common pattern.

Less information → more shrinkage.

Shrinkage is not “making areas equal.” It weights noisy area-specific information against a shared model. A data-rich area with a real excess keeps it.

section: 4.7 Unstructured heterogeneity: areas differ independently
text:
4.7 Unstructured heterogeneity: areas differ independently

In short. An unstructured random effect lets each area differ from the average, regardless of where it lies. It shrinks toward the overall mean but ignores geography.

\[
\log \theta_i = \alpha + v_i, \qquad v_i \sim \text{Normal}(0, \sigma_v^2)
\]

In words: each area’s log relative risk = a common level + its own deviation, and all deviations come from one shared bell curve.








What vᵢ captures
Area-specific deviations from the overall level of risk α


What it does not use
No neighbourhood information: vᵢ and vⱼ are independent a priori


Result
A shared distribution → partial pooling: shrinkage, but not spatial smoothing



Every area is shrunk toward the same global level, regardless of where it is. This is the fully Bayesian version of Session 2’s Empirical Bayes idea.

On the exam, be able to say: log θᵢ = α + vᵢ, vᵢ ~ N(0, σᵥ²), independent: partial pooling (shrinkage) but no spatial smoothing.

section: 4.8 Spatial smoothing: the CAR / ICAR prior
text:
4.8 Spatial smoothing: the CAR / ICAR prior

In short. The spatial (ICAR) prior says: an area’s hidden risk is probably close to the average of its neighbours’. Areas with many neighbours borrow more.
Think of it as: Guessing a house’s price from the houses on the same street.

Geography matters: neighbouring areas may share latent risk because they share

environment (air pollution, built environment, climate);
social context (deprivation, housing, local norms);
healthcare (access, catchments, diagnostic practice);
unmeasured factors (spatially patterned determinants not in X).

A spatial prior lets neighbouring areas share information about their underlying risks. In the conditional autoregressive form, an area’s latent effect is centred on its neighbours:
\[
u_i \mid u_{-i} \;\sim\; \text{Normal}\!\left(\frac{\sum_j w_{ij} u_j}{n_i},\; \frac{\sigma_u^2}{n_i}\right)
\]

In words: given its neighbours, an area’s spatial effect is expected to be near their average, and the more neighbours it has, the closer.








Part
Meaning




Neighbour mean Σⱼwᵢⱼuⱼ / nᵢ
The conditional centre is set by adjacent areas


nᵢ
Number (or total weight) of neighbours


Conditional variance σᵤ²/nᵢ
More neighbours → greater conditional precision (under the standard intrinsic CAR, ICAR, specification)



Intuition (slide 18). If A and C have similar spatial effects, the prior encourages B, between them, to be similar, unless B’s own data strongly disagree. This is borrowing strength through geography.
For this course: understand the mechanism; you do not need to derive the joint distribution.

On the exam, be able to say: ICAR: uᵢ given the others is normal with mean = average of the neighbours’ u and variance σᵤ²/nᵢ. More neighbours, more conditional precision. Borrowing strength through geography.

4.9 Partial pooling vs spatial smoothing

In short. Partial pooling borrows from all areas; spatial smoothing borrows from neighbours.

Key question 2: what is the difference between partial pooling and spatial smoothing?









Partial pooling (unstructured vᵢ)
Spatial smoothing (structured uᵢ)




Shrink toward
The global mean of all areas
The local mean of each area’s neighbours


Uses the map?
No: shuffling the areas on the map changes nothing
Yes: the neighbourhood graph W decides who borrows from whom


Captures

Smooth, clustered geographic patterns


Model

CAR / ICAR prior

Unstructured pooling shrinks every area toward the global mean, so noise is reduced but the map ignores geography. Spatial smoothing pulls each area toward its neighbours and recovers the true pattern best. Illustrative Poisson–gamma estimates, not a fitted BYM2 model.





Both shrink noisy small-area estimates. Spatial smoothing is a particular kind of partial pooling where the “group” an area borrows from is its neighbourhood.

On the exam, be able to say: Unstructured pooling shrinks toward the global mean and ignores the map; spatial smoothing shrinks toward the neighbourhood mean using W. Spatial smoothing is a geographic form of partial pooling.

section: 4.11 The Besag–York–Mollié (BYM) model: why both uᵢ and vᵢ
text:
4.11 The Besag–York–Mollié (BYM) model: why both uᵢ and vᵢ

In short. BYM = overall level + a spatial part (neighbours similar) + a non-spatial part (area-specific deviations).
Think of it as: Your height = what you share with your family + what is just you. Leave out either part and the explanation is wrong.

\[
Y_i \sim \text{Poisson}(E_i \theta_i), \qquad \log \theta_i = \alpha + u_i + v_i
\]

In words: log relative risk = common level + a part shared with neighbours + a part that is the area’s own.








Term
Role




α, overall level
Baseline log relative risk


uᵢ, structured
Spatially correlated component (ICAR): neighbouring areas borrow strength


vᵢ, unstructured
Independent area-specific heterogeneity



Two kinds of residual variation: spatial pattern + local noise. The model is named after Besag, York & Mollié (1991) (original paper, not required). Not all between-area variation needs to be spatially structured.
Key question 3: why include both structured and unstructured variation?

Structured uᵢ captures smooth or clustered geographic pattern: if one area is high, its neighbours are compatible with being high.
Unstructured vᵢ captures area-specific departures that do not need to resemble neighbours: local heterogeneity remains possible.
Without vᵢ, every residual difference is pushed into the spatial surface: a genuinely odd area would be forced to look like its neighbours (over-smoothing), and its neighbours distorted toward it.
Without uᵢ, geography is ignored: only global shrinkage.

Including both lets the data decide how much of the extra variation is spatial.
Both components represent unexplained variation in underlying risk; the distinction between them is statistical, not a claim about causes.

On the exam, be able to say: log θᵢ = α + uᵢ + vᵢ: uᵢ structured (ICAR), vᵢ unstructured. Without vᵢ everything is forced into the spatial surface (over-smoothing); without uᵢ geography is ignored.

section: 4.12 BYM2: separating overall variability from the spatial fraction
text:
4.12 BYM2: separating overall variability from the spatial fraction

In short. BYM2 rewrites BYM with two easy dials: τ, how much unexplained variation there is overall, and ρ, how much of it is spatial (0 = none, 1 = all).
Think of it as: A volume knob (τ: how much variation) and a balance knob (ρ: spatial vs non-spatial).

The problem with classic BYM (slide 23):

the marginal variability of uᵢ depends on the entire neighbourhood graph;
unlike vᵢ, its variance parameter does not directly represent marginal variability;
so how much residual variation is spatially structured is not directly interpretable, and priors are hard to set.

BYM2 reparameterizes the same idea:
\[
\log \theta_i = \alpha + \frac{1}{\sqrt{\tau}}\left(\sqrt{\rho}\; u_i^{*} + \sqrt{1 - \rho}\; v_i\right)
\]

In words: the same two parts as BYM, but mixed with a balance dial ρ (how much is spatial) and scaled by one volume dial 1/√τ (how much unexplained variation in total).








Parameter
Meaning




τ, overall precision
1/√τ controls the overall magnitude of residual heterogeneity. Larger τ → less residual variability; smaller τ → more


ρ, spatial fraction (mixing parameter), 0 ≤ ρ ≤ 1
ρ close to 1 → mostly structured; ρ close to 0 → mostly unstructured


uᵢ*, scaled spatial effect
Scaled so its variance has a stable interpretation across graphs (marginal variance about 1, like vᵢ)



This is the parameterization commonly used in modern Bayesian disease mapping. Original paper (not required): Riebler et al. (2016).
Interpreting ρ:








ρ ≈ 0
ρ ≈ 0.5
ρ ≈ 1




Residual heterogeneity is predominantly unstructured
Both components matter
Residual heterogeneity is dominated by geographic structure











Figure 3: What the BYM2 mixing parameter ρ does, simulated on a 12 × 12 grid. The same structured component u* (an ICAR draw) and unstructured component v, mixed as √ρ·u* + √(1−ρ)·v. With ρ = 0 the residual pattern is pure speckle; with ρ = 1 it is a smooth surface where neighbours resemble each other.






The slide’s question: if ρ is estimated as 0.9, does it mean 90% of disease cases are caused by spatial factors? No. ρ describes the residual latent variation (what remains after α and any covariates) on the BYM2 mixing scale: about 90% of the unexplained between-area variance is spatially structured. It says nothing about causes, nothing about cases, and nothing about variation that the covariates already explain. Also, BYM2’s ρ is not SAR’s ρ (3.4).


  Little residual variation overall, and most of it is spatially structured
  Much residual variation overall, and most of it is unstructured noise
  About 85% of all cases in the region are caused by spatial factors
  The covariates explain 85% of the variation between the areas
  τ is a precision, so a large τ means small residual variability. ρ near 1 means the residual variation that exists is mostly structured. ρ is not a causal share of cases and not an R².


On the exam, be able to say: BYM2: log θᵢ = α + (1/√τ)(√ρ·uᵢ* + √(1−ρ)·vᵢ). Larger τ = less residual variation. ρ is the share of residual variation that is spatially structured, not the share of disease caused by space.

section: 4.13 Priors: what are we putting priors on?
text:
4.13 Priors: what are we putting priors on?

In short. Priors go on the fixed effects, the overall variability and the spatial share. They decide how much and what kind of smoothing happens.








Part
Prior




Fixed effects α, β
Usually weakly informative or context-appropriate


Overall variability
Prior on τ (or the residual standard deviation 1/√τ)


Spatial mixing
Prior on ρ: expresses assumptions about the balance between structured and unstructured variation



For an introductory course, the key point is that priors regularize complexity. In applied work, consider prior sensitivity.

A prior on the overall variability influences how much smoothing occurs.
A prior on the spatial mixing influences the type of smoothing.


On the exam, be able to say: A prior on the overall variability affects how much smoothing occurs; a prior on the mixing parameter affects the type of smoothing. Priors regularize complexity; check sensitivity.

section: 4.14 Penalized-complexity (PC) priors
text:
4.14 Penalized-complexity (PC) priors

In short. PC priors prefer the simpler model unless the data clearly ask for more.

Marked optional depth on the slide.
Idea: start from a simpler base model (for BYM2: no residual variation, or no spatial structure) and penalise departures from it, so complexity is only used when the data support it. Original paper (not required): Simpson et al. (2017).
Why useful: hyperpriors can be stated as interpretable probability statements about plausible effect sizes, for example “P(residual SD > 1) = 0.01” or “P(ρ < 0.5) = 2/3”, rather than arbitrary values for a precision parameter. This is a common strategy with INLA and BYM2.

section: 4.15 Adding area-level covariates
text:
4.15 Adding area-level covariates

In short. Covariates can be added; exp(β) is the ratio of relative risks per unit of x. It is still an area-level, not causal, association.

\[
\log \theta_i = \alpha + X_i\beta + u_i + v_i
\]

In words: as BYM, plus a covariate; exp(β) is how many times higher the relative risk is per unit of x.








β
Area-level association with relative risk, on the log scale


exp(β)
Relative-risk ratio for a one-unit difference in X, conditional on the model


Caution
Spatial random effects do not automatically solve confounding or make β causal



Disease mapping and ecological regression overlap, but the inferential question matters: estimating each area’s risk (mapping) or estimating an area-level association (regression).
Spatial confounding. If X itself is spatially smooth, X and the spatial effect uᵢ can explain the same geographic pattern; adding uᵢ can then change β a lot, and neither version is automatically “right”.




On the exam, be able to say: exp(β) = relative-risk ratio for a one-unit difference in X, conditional on the model. Spatial random effects do not remove confounding or make β causal.

section: 4.16 What the posterior gives: relative risks, credible intervals, exceedance
text:
4.16 What the posterior gives: relative risks, credible intervals, exceedance

In short. For every area the model gives a whole distribution of possible risks. Summarise it as a point estimate, a credible interval and the probability that risk exceeds a threshold.









Output
What it is
Answers




Posterior mean / median of θᵢ
A smoothed point estimate; often mapped as relative risk
How high is the risk?


Credible interval (CrI)
Range of posterior uncertainty for θᵢ
How sure are we?


Exceedance probability P(θᵢ > c ∣ data)
Probability that θᵢ exceeds a scientifically meaningful threshold c
How likely is it that risk is elevated?



Bayesian disease mapping lets you map uncertainty, not only point estimates.
Interpreting a 95% credible interval. Example: posterior 95% CrI for θᵢ = [1.08, 1.42]. Under the fitted model and priors, 95% of the posterior probability for this area’s (latent) relative risk lies between 1.08 and 1.42.







A credible interval is
It is not




A probability statement about the parameter, given the data, model and prior
“95% of repeated confidence intervals contain the fixed true value” (the frequentist confidence interval statement)


Conditional on the model, data and prior assumptions
A statement free of assumptions



Exceedance probabilities.



Threshold
Meaning




c = 1
Probability that risk is above the reference level


c = 1.2
Probability that risk exceeds a 20% elevation



The choice of c should be tied to the scientific or decision context, not chosen to make a map look interesting. A map of exceedance probabilities can be more informative than thresholding a map of point estimates. A common convention flags areas with P(θᵢ > 1) above 0.8 or 0.95.

On the exam, be able to say: Posterior mean/median (smoothed RR), 95% credible interval (95% posterior probability given model and priors; not the confidence-interval statement), exceedance probability P(θᵢ > c | data).

text:
4.17 Higher posterior RR does not always mean stronger evidence

In short. A bigger estimate is not stronger evidence. Look at the interval and the exceedance probability too.





Area A
Area B




Posterior mean RR
1.30
1.20


95% CrI
0.75–2.00
1.10–1.31


P(RR > 1)
0.72

Figure 4: Posterior distributions for the two areas on slide 32, approximated by log-normal curves matching the slide’s 95% credible intervals. Area A’s distribution is wide, so a large share lies below 1. Area B’s is narrow and almost entirely above 1. The shaded area is the exceedance probability P(θ > 1); with this approximation A’s is 0.79 rather than the slide’s 0.72.





Which area gives stronger evidence of elevated risk? Area B. A has the higher point estimate, but its interval includes 1 and P(RR > 1) is only 0.72. B’s estimate is lower but precise, entirely above 1.
Key question 4: why might an area with a higher estimated RR have weaker evidence of elevated risk? Because magnitude and certainty are different dimensions. A small area (few expected cases) has a wide posterior: even after shrinkage its mean can be high while the data are compatible with no excess. A large area can have a modest but precisely estimated excess.

section: 4.23 Checkpoint: reconstruct the logic

4.23 Checkpoint: reconstruct the logic
Slide 41 asks you to explain each arrow in one sentence. Try it before opening the answer.





flowchart LR
  A["Observed /<br/>expected"] --> B["SMR"] --> C["Poisson<br/>model"] --> D["Partial<br/>pooling"] --> E["CAR /<br/>ICAR"] --> F["BYM2"] --> G["Posterior risk<br/>+ uncertainty"]


 Lecture map: each arrow is one step of the argument. Not causal. 









NoteModel answer: one sentence per arrow






Observed/expected → SMR: dividing observed by expected cases (from indirect standardization) gives a crude relative risk that adjusts for population composition.
SMR → Poisson model: treating Yᵢ ~ Poisson(Eᵢθᵢ) makes the SMR the maximum likelihood estimate of θᵢ and shows that its uncertainty depends on the size of the counts.
Poisson model → partial pooling: giving the log relative risks a common distribution lets data-poor areas borrow from the others, shrinking unstable SMRs toward the overall level.
Partial pooling → CAR/ICAR: a spatial prior centres each area’s effect on its neighbours’ effects, so borrowing happens locally (spatial smoothing).
CAR/ICAR → BYM2: combining a scaled structured effect with an unstructured effect, mixed by ρ and scaled by τ, lets the data decide how much residual variation is spatial.
BYM2 → posterior risk + uncertainty: the fitted model gives a posterior for each θᵢ, summarised as posterior means, credible intervals and exceedance probabilities.

section: 4.24 Take-home messages and key questions
text:
4.24 Take-home messages and key questions

Start with the estimand. Incidence, prevalence and standardized burden imply different data structures.
Raw small-area rates are noisy. SMRs can be extreme simply because denominators are small.
Bayesian models partially pool. Data-poor areas shrink more; data-rich areas keep more of their own signal.
BYM2 separates two ideas: overall heterogeneity and the fraction that is spatially structured.
Map uncertainty too. Posterior RR, credible intervals and exceedance probabilities answer different questions.







NoteWhy is Empirical Bayes (Session 2) not the same as BYM2?





EB estimates the prior from the data and shrinks every area toward one global rate, giving point estimates only. BYM2 is fully Bayesian: it puts priors on the hyperparameters, gives a full posterior for every area, and includes a spatial component, so areas are also smoothed toward their neighbours.









NoteWhen could spatial smoothing give a misleading map?





When neighbouring areas do not share the same underlying process: a real boundary (river, motorway, catchment border, policy line) or a sharp local hazard. The ICAR prior pulls the high area down and its neighbours up, blurring a genuine signal. Check the adjacency definition and compare with a less smoothed model.









NotePrevalence of diabetes from a health survey in each region: Poisson or Binomial?





Binomial: Yᵢ people with diabetes out of Nᵢ respondents, each yes/no, with target pᵢ (logit link). A BYM2 term can still be added to logit(pᵢ). Poisson would fit new diagnoses over person-time.

title: Session 2 — Disease Mapping and Spatial Patterns
text:
Session 2 moves from making maps to evaluating spatial patterns. It has two halves.
The first half is about maps of disease. How you classify a variable into colours changes what the reader sees, and crude rates from small populations are unstable: an area with 50 inhabitants can show a very high or very low rate purely by chance. The standardized mortality ratio (SMR) and Empirical Bayes smoothing are the first tools for this.
The second half formalises Tobler’s law. To ask whether nearby areas are similar, you first have to define who is a neighbour (a spatial weights matrix). Then Moran’s I measures global spatial autocorrelation, and local Moran’s I (LISA) says where the clusters and outliers are.
