title: Session 2 — Disease Mapping and Spatial Patterns
section: 2.1 Thematic (choropleth) maps and classification methods
text:
2.1 Thematic (choropleth) maps and classification methods

In short. A choropleth map colours areas by their value. Where you put the colour boundaries decides whether the same data look calm or alarming.

A thematic or choropleth map shows values with colours or patterns inside geographic areas. Two choices change the picture: the classification method (where the class boundaries go) and the number of classes.









Method
How the class breaks are chosen
Strength
Weakness




Quantile
Each class has the same number of areas (3 = tertiles, 4 = quartiles, 5 = quintiles)
Every colour is used equally; good for ranking
Very different values can share a class; close values can be split


Natural breaks (Jenks)
Breaks minimise variation within classes and maximise differences between them
Follows gaps in the data
Classes can hold very unequal numbers of areas; hard to compare maps


Equal intervals
The range is cut into classes of equal width
Easy to read
One extreme value can push most areas into one class


Manual intervals
You choose meaningful cut-offs (for example clinical thresholds)
Interpretable
Needs justification


Standard deviation
Values are expressed in SD units from the mean
Shows how far from average; spots outliers
Assumes a roughly symmetric distribution

Quantiles fill every class equally and make the map look busy; equal intervals put most areas in the lowest class; natural breaks follow gaps in the values. Same data, three impressions. (Natural breaks approximated here with one-dimensional k-means.)





There is no universally best method. It depends on the distribution of the data, the purpose of the map and the comparison you want the reader to make.

  Almost every area in the lowest class, a few in the top ones
  Each class holding the same number of areas, as in quintiles
  Classes chosen at the natural gaps between groups of values
  All areas coloured by how many SDs they lie from the mean

section: 2.4 Counts vs rates, and the problem of variance instability
text:
2.4 Counts vs rates, and the problem of variance instability

In short. Counts mostly show where people live; rates show risk. But rates from small populations jump around by chance, so the most extreme rates are often just the smallest areas.
Think of it as: A basketball player who scores 2 of 2 shots has 100%, yet you would trust 450 of 500 (90%) much more.

Two kinds of variables behave differently on a map:









Spatially extensive
Spatially intensive




Depends on population size?
Yes
No, standardized by population


Example
Number of cases or deaths
Rate or risk: cases per population


What a map shows
Mostly where people live
Where the risk is high



Mapping counts therefore mostly reproduces a population map: big cities have the most cases. Crude rates fix this, but bring a new problem.
Variance instability. For area i with observed cases Oᵢ and population at risk Pᵢ, the crude risk is rᵢ = Oᵢ / Pᵢ. If the underlying risk is πᵢ,
\[
\operatorname{Var}(r_i) = \frac{\pi_i (1 - \pi_i)}{P_i}.
\]

In words: the uncertainty of a crude rate is the true risk times one minus it, divided by the population: the fewer people, the noisier the rate.

Small Pᵢ → large variance → unstable crude estimates. Areas with small populations show very high or very low crude rates simply because of sampling variability. This motivates smoothing.
The slide’s question: with the same underlying πᵢ, which area has the more variable observed risk, Pᵢ = 100 or Pᵢ = 10,000? Pᵢ = 100: its variance is 100 times larger (its standard deviation 10 times larger).





Simulated: 300 areas that all share the same true risk of 1%. Left: crude rates against population size. The most extreme rates, both high and low, all belong to small areas, a ‘funnel’. Right: the map-maker’s view, the 15 highest crude rates; nearly all are small areas with no real excess risk.





  Small populations give unstable rates that scatter in both directions
  Rural areas have a genuinely more extreme mix of cancer risk factors
  Counts were mapped instead of rates, so population size dominates
  The classification method put rural areas in the extreme classes
  Extremes in both directions in small areas is the signature of variance instability. A real rural risk factor would push rates one way, not both ways.


On the exam, be able to say: Counts are spatially extensive (depend on population size); rates are intensive. Var(rᵢ) = πᵢ(1 − πᵢ)/Pᵢ, so small populations give unstable crude rates: variance instability. This motivates smoothing.

text:
2.5 Comparing areas with the SMR (excess risk)

In short. The SMR compares what happened with what would have happened if the area had the reference risk: SMR = observed ÷ expected.

An excess risk map compares each area’s rate with a reference risk (national or regional). The reference risk is estimated from all observations pooled:
\[
\hat\pi = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} O_i}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} P_i} = \frac{\text{total events}}{\text{total population at risk}}.
\]
Expected count and standardized mortality ratio (SMR):
\[
E_i = \hat\pi \times P_i, \qquad \text{SMR}_i = \frac{O_i}{E_i} = \frac{O_i}{\hat\pi P_i} = \frac{r_i}{\hat\pi}.
\]

In words: expected cases = the reference risk times the area’s population; the SMR is observed divided by expected.

The slide’s two questions:

Is π̂ equal to the average of all rates? No. π̂ is a population-weighted average: total events over total population. The simple mean of the area rates gives every area the same weight, so a few small areas with extreme rates can pull it far away. They coincide only if all areas have the same population.
How to interpret SMRᵢ > 1? Area i had more events than expected if the reference risk applied there. SMR = 1.3 means 30% more than expected. It is not, on its own, evidence of a real excess: a small Eᵢ makes the SMR unstable (Session 4).


Slide practice. Overall cancer risk 10%. Area A has 1,000 residents at risk; 20 get cancer.








Approach
Calculation
SMR

E = 1000 × 10% = 100; SMR = 20 / 100

crude rate = 20 / 1000 = 2%; SMR = 2% / 10%

Expected counts can also use stratum-specific reference risks (by age and sex): indirect standardization, worked through in Session 4.




On the exam, be able to say: Eᵢ = π̂ × Pᵢ with π̂ = total events / total population (a population-weighted average, not the mean of the rates). SMR = O/E; SMR > 1 means more events than expected.

section: 2.6 Empirical Bayes smoothing
text:
2.6 Empirical Bayes smoothing

In short. EB smoothing pulls each crude rate toward the overall rate, more strongly the smaller the population. Reliable areas keep their own rate; noisy ones borrow from the average.
Think of it as: Restaurant ratings. A 5.0 from 3 reviews is less convincing than a 4.6 from 3,000, so a sensible guess for the first restaurant moves toward the typical rating.

Idea: replace each crude rate by a weighted average of the area’s own crude rate and the overall (reference) rate:
\[
\hat\pi_i^{EB} = w_i\, r_i + (1 - w_i)\, \theta, \qquad w_i = \frac{\sigma^2}{\sigma^2 + \mu / P_i}.
\]

In words: the smoothed rate is a weighted average of the area’s own rate and the reference rate. The weight compares real differences between areas (σ²) with noise (μ/Pᵢ): little noise → trust the area, much noise → trust the reference.








Symbol
Meaning




rᵢ
Crude rate in area i


θ (= μ)
Prior estimate: the reference rate (overall average or another standard)


σ²
Variance of the true rates between areas (how much real variation there is)


μ / Pᵢ
Approximately the sampling variance of rᵢ: large when Pᵢ is small


wᵢ
Weight on the area’s own data, between 0 and 1



Reading the weight. wᵢ compares real between-area variation (σ²) with noise (μ/Pᵢ):

large, informative area: μ/Pᵢ is tiny, wᵢ ≈ 1 → little shrinkage, the area keeps its own rate;
small, uninformative area: μ/Pᵢ is large, wᵢ is small → strong shrinkage toward the reference rate.









Figure 2: Empirical Bayes smoothing, simulated: 40 areas whose true risks vary moderately around 1%. Left: each grey line shows how far a crude rate (orange) moves to its EB estimate (blue). Small areas are pulled almost all the way to the reference rate; large areas barely move. Right: the weight w on the area’s own rate grows with population.





EB smoothing reduces the influence of unstable extreme estimates from small populations.

“Empirical Bayes is a Bayesian method.” Not quite. The prior (θ and σ²) is estimated from the same data rather than specified beforehand, and the method produces point estimates without a full posterior distribution. It borrows the Bayesian idea of shrinkage. (The same trick is used in moderated t-tests for gene expression: small samples get their variance shrunk.) Fully Bayesian disease mapping is Session 4.

Three maps of the same data (slides 17–18): a raw rate map, an excess risk map (SMR) and an EB smoothed map can look quite different. In the raw and excess risk box maps, small areas often appear as outliers; after EB smoothing, many of them move back toward the middle and the remaining outliers are more trustworthy.









TipWhen to use EB smoothing



When areas differ a lot in population size and the goal is a map of risk that is not dominated by small-area noise. It is quick and needs no model fitting.








WarningLimitations



It ignores geography: every area is shrunk toward the same global mean, not toward its neighbours (spatial EB versions exist). It gives no full uncertainty for each area. A genuinely high-risk small area is pulled toward the mean too, so real local excesses can be hidden.



On the exam, be able to say: EB estimate = wᵢ·rᵢ + (1 − wᵢ)·θ with wᵢ = σ²/(σ² + μ/Pᵢ). Small areas get small weights (strong shrinkage), large areas keep their own rate. The prior is estimated from the data, so it is not fully Bayesian.

section: 2.7 Spatial autocorrelation and the null of spatial randomness
text:
2.7 Spatial autocorrelation and the null of spatial randomness

In short. Spatial autocorrelation asks: are nearby areas more alike than they would be if the values had been scattered at random over the map?
Think of it as: Shuffle the map like a deck of cards many times. If the real map is more clustered than almost all shuffled maps, the pattern is not chance.

Spatial autocorrelation formalises Tobler’s law: the correlation of a variable with itself across space.





Three 8 × 8 patterns with the same number of black and white cells (as on slide 20, after O’Sullivan and Unwin 2002). Moran’s I uses binary rook weights.




Testing. A test statistic summarises the data and is compared with its distribution under the null hypothesis. For spatial autocorrelation the null is spatial randomness: the observed values are not systematically associated with their locations. Any arrangement of the values over the map would be equally likely.
That suggests a direct test: randomly permute (reshuffle) the values over the locations many times, compute the statistic each time, and see where the observed value falls.
To measure autocorrelation you need two kinds of similarity at once:

attribute similarity: are two values alike? (for Moran’s I, the product of deviations from the mean, zᵢzⱼ);
locational similarity: are the two areas neighbours? (the spatial weight wᵢⱼ).


On the exam, be able to say: Positive autocorrelation: similar values cluster; negative: neighbours differ (checkerboard). The null hypothesis is spatial randomness, tested by comparing with random permutations.

2.9 Spatial weights: distance bands and k-nearest neighbours

In short. Neighbours can also be defined by distance: everyone within a set distance (distance band), or each area’s k nearest. KNN guarantees that everyone has neighbours, but the relation is not symmetric.
Think of it as: KNN is like “your four closest friends”: you may be on their list, or not.

Distance-based weights use the distance between points (or area centroids).
Distance metrics








Metric
Formula / idea
Use when




Euclidean (straight line)
\(d_{ij} = \sqrt{(x_i - x_j)^2 + (y_i - y_j)^2}\)
Coordinates are projected (on a plane, in metres)

Distance along the Earth’s curved surface
Unprojected longitude/latitude



Distance-band weights. i and j are neighbours whenever j is within a critical distance of i. The result is symmetric. To avoid isolates, the threshold is often set to the largest nearest-neighbour distance (so every area has at least one neighbour), but then areas in dense clusters can get very many neighbours.
Isolates are areas with no neighbours. They drop out of all spatial analyses (autocorrelation tests, spatial regression), although they are fine in non-spatial analysis. Ignoring them is a problem for spatially lagged variables and local statistics.
k-nearest-neighbour (KNN) weights. Choose k (say 4); each area gets its k nearest neighbours (by centroid distance).

Connects every area: no isolates.
Not symmetric: B can be among A’s 4 nearest without A being among B’s 4 nearest (B may sit in a dense cluster). It can be made symmetric, for example \(w^*_{ij} = (w_{ij} + w_{ji})/2\).
Ties: several areas at the same distance; choose randomly or include all.

2.10 Describing a weights matrix: connectivity histogram and graph

In short. Two quick checks of a weights matrix: how many neighbours each area has (histogram) and a picture of the links (graph).

Two diagnostics show what a weights matrix looks like:

Connectivity histogram: how many areas have 1, 2, 3, … neighbours.
Connectivity graph: a line between the centroids of every pair of neighbours.

The slides’ questions:
What does the histogram look like with KNN weights? A single bar at k: every area has exactly k neighbours. (If you symmetrize the KNN matrix, some areas gain neighbours and the histogram spreads to the right of k.)
Which graph suggests KNN and which suggests a distance band? With a distance band, dense areas (cities) have very many links, sparse areas have few, and isolated points may have none. With KNN, every point has the same number of links, even remote points, which reach out with long lines to their nearest neighbours.

section: 2.11 Global Moran’s I
text:
2.11 Global Moran’s I

In short. Moran’s I is one number for the whole map: positive when neighbours are alike, negative when they differ, close to zero when there is no pattern. Whether it is unusual is judged against shuffled maps.

\[
I = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n} w_{ij}\, z_i z_j \,/\, S_0}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} z_i^2 \,/\, n},
\qquad z_i = x_i - \bar x, \qquad S_0 = \sum_i\sum_j w_{ij}.
\]

In words: for every pair of neighbours, multiply how far each is from the mean; average these products over all neighbour pairs and divide by the overall variance. Mostly positive products (high next to high, low next to low) → I > 0.

Reading it. The numerator is a cross-product between each value and its neighbours (attribute similarity × locational similarity), averaged over all neighbour pairs. The denominator is the variance. So Moran’s I is like a correlation between a variable and its spatial lag.



zᵢ and its neighbours’ zⱼ
Product zᵢzⱼ
Contribution

+
Positive


Both below the mean (low next to low)
+
Positive

−
Negative



Inference. H₀: spatial randomness. Two ways to judge whether the observed I is unusual:








Approach
How
Pros / cons




Analytical
Normal approximation with the theoretical mean and variance of I
Fast; sensitive to distributional assumptions


Permutation (computational)
Randomly reshuffle the values over the areas many times, compute I each time, compare the observed I with this reference distribution → pseudo p-value
More robust; limited to the actual sample. More permutations (999 rather than 99) give more stable results



Moran’s I depends on the weights: the same data with another W give another I.

“Under the null hypothesis Moran’s I equals 0.” Its expected value under spatial randomness is \(E[I] = -1/(n-1)\), slightly negative. For 100 areas that is about −0.01, so in practice “about 0”. With very few areas the difference matters.

The pseudo p-value from R permutations is (number of permuted I ≥ observed I, plus 1) / (R + 1). With 999 permutations the smallest possible value is 1/1000 = 0.001.

section: 2.13 Local spatial autocorrelation: LISA and local Moran’s I
text:
2.13 Local spatial autocorrelation: LISA and local Moran’s I

In short. Global Moran’s I says whether there is clustering; LISA says where. Each area gets its own statistic and p-value, and significant areas are labelled HH, LL, HL or LH.










Global
Local




Question
Is there spatial clustering?
Where, and what type?


Output
One number for the whole map
One statistic and one p-value per area


Measures
Moran’s I (Geary’s C)
LISA, for example local Moran’s I; local Geary


Finds
Overall clustering
Hot spots, cold spots and spatial outliers









NoteDeeper: the formal definition of a LISA





LISA (local indicator of spatial association, Anselin 1995) must:

give a statistic for each location with an assessment of significance;
be such that the sum of the local statistics is proportional to the global statistic.

Generic local form Σⱼ wᵢⱼ f(xᵢ, xⱼ); generic global form Σᵢ Σⱼ wᵢⱼ f(xᵢ, xⱼ).



Local Moran’s I:
\[
I_i = \frac{z_i \sum_j w_{ij} z_j}{\sum_i z_i^2 } ,
\]

In words: an area’s own deviation from the mean times its neighbours’ deviations. Large and positive = the area and its neighbours are on the same side of the mean (a cluster); negative = opposite sides (an outlier).

the area’s own deviation times the weighted sum of its neighbours’ deviations. Global Moran’s I corresponds to the average of the local statistics (their sum is proportional to the global I).
Significance by conditional permutation. As for the global test, except that zᵢ is held fixed at location i and only the other values are reshuffled over its neighbours. This gives a pseudo p-value for each area.
Two maps come out of a LISA analysis:

a significance map: areas coloured by pseudo p-value (0.05, 0.01, 0.001);
a cluster map: the significant areas coloured by type: High-High and Low-Low clusters, High-Low and Low-High outliers.









Figure 6: LISA, simulated. Left: the rate map. Middle: the significance map, pseudo p-values from conditional permutation. Right: the cluster map, the significant areas coloured by type. The one HL area is an odd high value placed inside a low region: a spatial outlier.











WarningInterpreting a cluster map



“High” and “low” are relative to the mean of the variable. A High-High area is significant together with its neighbours: the cluster is the core area and its neighbours, not just the coloured area. With many areas, some will be significant at 0.05 by chance (multiple testing); stricter cut-offs (0.01, 0.001) or false discovery rate adjustments are often used. And LISA on raw rates inherits variance instability: small areas can produce spurious clusters.



  Its value is below the mean while its neighbours’ values are above it
  Its value is below the mean and so are those of its neighbours
  Its value is above the mean while its neighbours’ are below it
  It belongs to a cold spot that is surrounded by a hot spot
  The first word describes the area itself, the second its neighbours (spatial lag), both relative to the mean. Low-High is a spatial outlier: a low value among high neighbours, which is negative local autocorrelation.







TipWhen to use global vs local statistics



Global Moran’s I first, to ask whether there is clustering at all. LISA when you need to locate clusters and outliers, for example for surveillance or to target resources. Choose and report W, and check robustness to another W.


Read more: GeoDa workbook, Local spatial autocorrelation (source of the significance and cluster maps on the slides).

On the exam, be able to say: LISA gives a local statistic with significance for each location, and the local statistics sum (proportionally) to the global one. Local Moran’s I is tested by conditional permutation; results are shown in significance and cluster maps.

section: 2.14 Session summary and key questions
text:
2.14 Session summary and key questions





flowchart LR
  A["Map counts"] -->|"population dominates"| B["Map crude rates"]
  B -->|"small areas unstable"| C["SMR / EB smoothing"]
  C --> D["Is there clustering?<br/>define W → global Moran's I"]
  D --> E["Where is it?<br/>LISA cluster map"]


 Lecture map: how the session’s problems lead into each other. Not causal. 









NoteWhy can a map of counts and a map of crude rates show different patterns?





Counts are spatially extensive: they grow with population, so the count map mostly shows where people live. Crude rates are intensive: they divide by population and show risk. A big city can have the most cases but an average rate; a small municipality can have few cases but a high rate.









NoteWhy does EB smoothing shrink small areas more than large ones?





The weight wᵢ = σ²/(σ² + μ/Pᵢ) compares true between-area variance with sampling noise μ/Pᵢ. In small areas the noise term is large, so wᵢ is small and the estimate is pulled toward the reference rate. In large areas the crude rate is already precise and keeps most of its weight.









NoteWhat is the null hypothesis for Moran’s I, and how does a permutation test use it?





Spatial randomness: values are unrelated to location, so any reshuffling of the values over the areas is equally likely. Reshuffling many times and computing I each time gives the distribution of I under H₀; the share of permuted values at least as large as the observed I is the pseudo p-value.









NoteCan global Moran’s I be close to zero even though there are local clusters?





Yes. Local positive (clusters) and negative (outliers) associations can cancel out, or a few strong clusters may be diluted by many random areas. That is why LISA is used to look locally.

title: Glossary
section: A–C
text:
A–C

Accessibility (the five A’s)

Access as the fit between clients and the health system (Penchansky & Thomas 1981): availability, accessibility, affordability, acceptability, accommodation. Spatial measures capture mainly the first two. S6 §6.9

Averages chart

GeoDa tool that tests the difference in means between spatially selected and unselected areas; with two groups the F-test equals a t-test. S6 §6.6

Bandwidth (LOWESS)

Fraction of the x-range used in each local fit. Larger bandwidth gives a smoother curve; smaller gives a wigglier one. S6 §6.4

Brushing and linking

Selecting observations in one view (map, histogram, scatter plot) highlights them in all linked views; brushing moves the selection box and updates the views. S6 §6.2

Buffer analysis

Counting features near an area as well as within it, using zones of fixed distance (buffers) around facilities or areas. S6 §6.11

BYM model (Besag–York–Mollié)

Disease-mapping model log θᵢ = α + uᵢ + vᵢ with a spatially structured effect uᵢ (ICAR) and an unstructured effect vᵢ. S4 §4.11

BYM2

Reparameterization of BYM: log θᵢ = α + (1/√τ)(√ρ·uᵢ* + √(1−ρ)·vᵢ). τ is the overall precision, ρ the spatial fraction, uᵢ* the scaled spatial effect. S4 §4.12

Box map

Extreme value map using box-plot categories: lower outlier, < 25%, 25–50%, 50–75%, > 75%, upper outlier, with fences Q1 − hinge·IQR and Q3 + hinge·IQR (hinge 1.5 or 3). S2 §2.2

CAR / ICAR prior

(Intrinsic) conditional autoregressive prior: each area’s latent effect is normal around the mean of its neighbours’ effects, with variance σ²/nᵢ. More neighbours, more conditional precision. S4 §4.8

Choropleth (thematic) map

Map that shows values with colours or patterns inside areas. S2 §2.1

Chow test

Tests whether regression coefficients are equal in two (or more) subsets, for example selected and unselected areas or rural/suburban/urban regimes. S6 §6.7

Cluster analysis

Unsupervised grouping of observations so that similarity is high within and low between clusters. S6 §6.18

Co-location map

Extension of the unique value map that shows where several characteristics overlap. S2 §2.3

Connectivity histogram / graph

Diagnostics of a weights matrix: the distribution of the number of neighbours, and lines between neighbouring centroids. S2 §2.10

Container method

Accessibility measured as the count of facilities inside a unit (point-in-polygon) or within buffers. Border- and buffer-size dependent. S6 §6.11

Contiguity weights (rook, queen)

Neighbours share a boundary (rook) or a boundary or corner (queen). Queen gives at least as many neighbours. Can be higher order. S2 §2.8

Coordinate reference system (CRS)

Specifies how coordinates relate to places on Earth and, if projected, how the surface is flattened. Identified by EPSG codes. S1 §1.3

Credible interval (CrI)

Interval containing a given posterior probability (e.g. 95%) for a parameter, conditional on model, data and prior. Not the repeated-sampling statement of a confidence interval. S4 §4.16

Curse of dimensionality

With many variables data become sparse, more data are needed and computation grows; methods that work in few dimensions may fail (Bellman 1961). S6 §6.15

title: Glossary
section: D–I
text:
D–I

DeSO (demographic statistical areas)

Sweden’s small statistical areas, designed to hold roughly 700–2,700 inhabitants. S1 §1.4

Difference-in-differences (DiD)

Effect = (treated post − treated pre) − (control post − control pre). Removes time-invariant differences and common shocks; assumes parallel trends. S6 §6.26

Direct, indirect and total impacts

In SAR: the effect of x on the own area including feedback (direct), on other areas through the network (indirect, spillover), and their sum (total = β/(1−ρ) with row-standardized W). S3 §3.5

Distance-band weights

i and j are neighbours if within a critical distance. Symmetric; dense areas get many neighbours. S2 §2.9

Ecological fallacy

Incorrect inference about individuals from group-level data (Robinson 1950). S1 §1.11

Elbow plot

Within-cluster sum of squares plotted against K; choose K where the decrease slows sharply (the kink). S6 §6.19

Empirical Bayes (EB) smoothing

π̂ᵢ = wᵢrᵢ + (1 − wᵢ)θ with wᵢ = σ²/(σ² + μ/Pᵢ): crude rates shrunk toward a reference rate, more for small populations. The prior is estimated from the data. S2 §2.6

EPSG code

Standard number for a CRS. EPSG:4326 = WGS 84 (degrees); EPSG:3006 = SWEREF 99 TM (metres, Sweden). S1 §1.3

ESDA (exploratory spatial data analysis)

Linked maps and statistical graphs used to detect patterns, outliers and heterogeneity and to generate hypotheses. S6 §6.2

Exceedance probability

Posterior probability that a relative risk exceeds a threshold c, P(θᵢ > c ∣ data). S4 §4.16

Expected count Eᵢ

Cases expected in area i at reference rates: Eᵢ = π̂·Pᵢ, or Σₐ nᵢₐ r*ₐ with strata (indirect standardization). S2 §2.5, S4 §4.3

Exposure lag WD (spatial treatment exposure)

Gᵢ = Σⱼ wᵢⱼDⱼ: the weighted share of area i’s neighbours that are treated. Not the same as the outcome lag WY. S6 §6.28

Extensive vs intensive variable

Extensive depends on population size (counts); intensive is standardized by population (rates). S2 §2.4

Floating catchment area (2SFCA)

Access measure in two steps: supply-to-population ratio for each facility within its catchment, then the sum of these ratios over the facilities each location can reach. Extensions: E2SFCA, KD2SFCA, M2SFCA, 3SFCA, RAAM. S6 §6.13

Geary’s C

Alternative measure of spatial autocorrelation based on squared differences between neighbours. S1 §1.12

Geocoding

Converting addresses to coordinates (longitude, latitude). Can fail or be wrong. S1 §1.4

GeoDa

Free software for exploratory spatial data analysis. S1 §1.14

Geographic regression discontinuity (RDD)

Causal design comparing locations just on either side of a policy boundary. S6 §6.25

GeoJSON

Open standard text format for points, lines and polygons. S1 §1.2

GeoPackage (.gpkg)

Single-file spatial data format holding geometry, attributes and CRS together. S5 §5.7

GIS

Geographic information systems: tools for storing, linking, mapping and analysing data by location. S1 §1.14

Gravity potential

Access as the sum of facility sizes weighted by a distance-decay function, for example Aᵢ = Σⱼ Sⱼ / dᵢⱼ^β. S6 §6.12

INLA

Integrated nested Laplace approximation: fast approximation of posterior marginals for latent Gaussian models such as BYM2, without MCMC. S4 §4.21

Instrumental variables (IV)

Causal design using plausibly exogenous variation in exposure that affects the outcome only through the exposure. S6 §6.25

Isolate

Area with no neighbours in a weights matrix; it drops out of spatial analyses. S2 §2.9, S4 §4.19

title: Glossary
section: K–M
text:
K–M

K-means

Exact clustering into K groups using squared Euclidean distance dᵢⱼ² = Σᵥ (xᵢᵥ − xⱼᵥ)², with iterative relocation to minimize within-cluster dissimilarity. S6 §6.18

k-nearest-neighbour (KNN) weights

Each area’s k nearest centroids are its neighbours. No isolates; not symmetric; ties possible. S2 §2.9

LISA (local indicator of spatial association)

Local statistic for each location with a significance assessment, whose sum is proportional to the global statistic. Local Moran’s I is one. S2 §2.13

LM tests (LM-lag, LM-error, robust)

Tests on an OLS fit of whether a spatial lag or spatial error term is supported. Robust versions help when both are significant. S3 §3.10

Local Moran’s I

Iᵢ = zᵢ Σⱼ wᵢⱼ zⱼ / Σ zᵢ². Tested by conditional permutation; classifies significant areas as High-High, Low-Low, High-Low, Low-High. S2 §2.13

LOWESS

Locally weighted scatter plot smoother: local slopes on small x-intervals, nearby points weighted more, joined into a smooth curve. S6 §6.3

Matching

Causal design comparing treated and untreated areas with similar measured characteristics. S6 §6.25

MAUP (modifiable areal unit problem)

Results change when the spatial units change (scale or zoning), even with the same underlying data. S1 §1.10

Minimum distance

Accessibility as the distance from an origin to the nearest facility. Ignores capacity and competition. S6 §6.12

Moran scatter plot

Each area’s value (x) against its spatial lag (y); the slope is Moran’s I with row-standardized weights. S2 §2.12

Moran’s I (global)

I = (n/S₀) ΣᵢΣⱼ wᵢⱼ zᵢzⱼ / Σ zᵢ². Positive: clustering; negative: dispersion; E[I] = −1/(n−1) under spatial randomness. S2 §2.11

title: Glossary
section: N–R
text:
N–R

Neumann series

(I − ρW)⁻¹ = I + ρW + ρ²W² + …: how an effect propagates through the spatial network in SAR. S3 §3.5

Offset

A term with coefficient fixed at 1 in a Poisson model (log Eᵢ or log person-time), so the model describes a rate or relative risk. S4 §4.2

Parallel trends

DiD assumption: without the intervention, treated and control groups would have changed equally. About counterfactual changes, not equal baseline levels. S6 §6.26

Partial pooling

Area estimates drawn from a shared distribution, so each is a compromise between its own data and the common pattern. S4 §4.6

Penalized-complexity (PC) prior

Prior that penalises departures from a simpler base model; hyperpriors stated as probabilities about interpretable quantities. S4 §4.14

Percentile map

Extreme value map with fixed classes < 1%, 1–10%, 10–50%, 50–90%, 90–99%, > 99%. S2 §2.2

Permutation test (pseudo p-value)

Reshuffle values over locations many times to get the distribution of a statistic under spatial randomness; pseudo p = (count ≥ observed + 1)/(R + 1). S2 §2.11

Point-in-polygon

Counting events, places or facilities inside each area. S6 §6.11

Principal components analysis (PCA)

Replaces correlated variables with a few orthogonal linear combinations (components) that keep as much variance as possible. S6 §6.16

Projected vs geographic CRS

Geographic: longitude/latitude in degrees. Projected: flat coordinates, usually metres, needed for distances and areas. S1 §1.3

Raster vs vector data

Raster: a grid of cells with values. Vector: points, lines and polygons stored as coordinates. S1 §1.1

Relative risk θᵢ

Ratio of an area’s underlying risk to the reference: θᵢ = 1 as expected, > 1 elevated. S4 §4.3

Residual Moran’s I

Moran’s I of regression residuals; detects remaining spatial structure but does not distinguish SAR from SEM. S3 §3.9

Risk classification (0.8 rule)

Classifying areas by exceedance probability: P(RR > 1) > 0.8 elevated, < 0.2 lower, otherwise uncertain (Richardson et al. 2004). Conservative. S5 §5.6

Row standardization

Dividing each row of W by its sum, so (Wy)ᵢ is the average of i’s neighbours. S2 §2.8

title: Glossary
section: S–Z
text:
S–Z

SDOH index

An index of social determinants of health, for example the four PCA components of Kolak et al. (2020): SES, MOB, URB, MICA. S6 §6.17

Shapefile

ESRI format of at least four files in the same folder: .shp (geometry), .shx (index), .dbf (attributes), .prj (projection). S1 §1.2

Shrinkage

Noisy area estimates moving toward a common pattern; more for less informative areas. S4 §4.6

SMR (standardized mortality ratio)

Observed / expected count. SMR > 1: more events than expected. The crude (unsmoothed) estimate of θᵢ. S2 §2.5, S4 §4.4

Spatial autocorrelation

Correlation of a variable with itself across space; tested against the null of spatial randomness. S2 §2.7

Spatial clustering

Clustering that considers locational as well as attribute similarity, by adding coordinates as variables or by multi-objective weighting; gives compact regions. S6 §6.20

Spatial confounding

Covariates and latent spatial effects sharing similar geographic patterns, so their effects are hard to separate. S4 §4.15

Spatial data

Information + location. S1 §1.1

Spatial dependence

Nearby observations are more similar (or related) than distant ones; Tobler’s first law. S1 §1.12

Spatial epidemiology

Description and analysis of geographic variation in disease with respect to demographic, environmental, behavioural, socioeconomic, genetic and infectious risk factors; more broadly, describing, analysing and intervening on spatial patterns of health. S1 §1.6

Spatial error model (SEM)

y = Xβ + u, u = λWu + ε: spatial dependence in the errors; λ measures it. S3 §3.7

Spatial heterogeneity

Processes or relationships that differ across locations. S1 §1.12

Spatial interference

An intervention in one area changes outcomes in another (spillover). Not the same as spatial dependence. S6 §6.22

Spatial lag Wy

Weighted summary of the neighbours’ values; with row-standardized W, the neighbour average. S3 §3.3

Spatial lag model (SAR)

y = ρWy + Xβ + ε: an area’s outcome depends on neighbours’ outcomes; ρ measures it. S3 §3.4

Spatial randomness

The null hypothesis that values are not systematically associated with their locations. S2 §2.7

Spatial regime model

Regression with separate coefficients for spatially defined subsets (regimes), for example rural, suburban, urban; models spatial heterogeneity. S6 §6.20

Spatial smoothing

Borrowing strength from neighbouring areas so each estimate is pulled toward its neighbours. S4 §4.8

Spatial weights matrix W

Matrix recording whether (or how strongly) each pair of areas are neighbours; wᵢᵢ = 0. S2 §2.8

Spatially structured confounding

Geographic factors (for example deprivation) that influence both exposure and outcome. S6 §6.22

Structural break

A point where the relationship between variables changes; a bend in a LOWESS curve or different slopes in subsets may suggest one. S6 §6.3

Tobler’s first law of geography

“Things closer together are more similar than things further apart.” S1 §1.12

Unstructured random effect vᵢ

Independent area effect vᵢ ~ N(0, σ²): partial pooling toward the global mean without using geography. S4 §4.7

Variance instability

Crude rates from small populations have large variance, π(1−π)/P, and produce spurious extremes. S2 §2.4

Within-cluster sum of squares (WCSS)

Sum of squared distances from observations to their cluster centre; always decreases with K. S6 §6.19

title: Exam practice
section: Written questions
text:
Written questions

Session 1: spatial data and key issues






NoteW1. Define spatial epidemiology and explain what Morrison et al. (2024) add to the classical definition.





Spatial epidemiology is the description and analysis of geographic variation in disease with respect to demographic, environmental, behavioural, socioeconomic, genetic and infectious risk factors (Elliott & Wartenberg 2004). Morrison et al. broaden it: the field applies theory and methods from epidemiology, geography and statistics to describe spatial distributions, analyze causes, inform intervention and improve health. Their review found 0 intervention studies among 482 papers, so the broader definition is a call to move from maps to mechanisms to action.









NoteW2. What is the modifiable areal unit problem (MAUP)? Give an example and one way to reduce it.





Changing the spatial units (their size: scale effect; or their boundaries: zoning effect) can change statistical results and interpretations, even though the underlying individual data are the same. Example: the correlation between deprivation and mortality is stronger across counties than across DeSO areas. Ways to deal with it: report the unit, repeat the analysis at several scales, choose units that match the mechanism, or use regular grids (hexagons) where data allow.









NoteW3. Distinguish the ecological fallacy from the MAUP.





Both arise from aggregation. The ecological fallacy is drawing conclusions about individuals from group-level data (a high-crime region does not mean its residents are criminals). The MAUP is about area-level results depending on how areas are drawn. An area-level association can be stable across zonings and still be an ecological fallacy if applied to people.









NoteW4. Explain spatial dependence and spatial heterogeneity, with one health example each.





Spatial dependence: nearby observations are more similar than distant ones (Tobler’s first law), for example neighbouring municipalities have similar obesity prevalence. Spatial heterogeneity: processes or relationships differ by location, so one global model can miss local patterns, for example the effect of temperature on admissions differs between north and south. Dependence is about similarity of values; heterogeneity is about differences in relationships.









NoteW5. Why must layers be in the same coordinate reference system before they are joined, and when do you need a projected CRS?





Coordinates are only meaningful relative to a CRS; two layers in different CRSs describe the same place with different numbers and will not overlay, so joins and overlays fail or are wrong. A projected CRS (for example SWEREF 99 TM, EPSG:3006, in metres) is needed for distances and areas, because in a geographic CRS (EPSG:4326, degrees) a degree is not a fixed distance.









NoteW6. [instructor] In the John Snow activity: what was the research question, what were the competing hypotheses, and what spatial data were used?





Question: what caused the 1854 cholera outbreak in Soho, and how is cholera transmitted? Hypotheses: miasma (bad air) versus waterborne transmission. Data: locations of cholera deaths (points by household) and of public water pumps on a street map, plus water-company supply by household. Using Morrison’s framework, Snow described (map), analyzed (comparison of water sources, informative exceptions) and intervened (removing the Broad Street pump handle).









NoteW7. Name three sources of bias in spatial health data and how each could distort a map.





Geographically varying reporting (under-reporting regions look healthy); geocoding failure (dropped or misplaced cases, often more common in rural areas, so missing not at random); boundary changes (rates before and after are not comparable); small populations (unstable rates that produce spurious extremes). Any of these can create apparent patterns that reflect data collection, not risk.





Session 2: maps, smoothing and autocorrelation






NoteW8. [instructor] Why can mapping counts and mapping crude rates produce different spatial patterns?





Counts are spatially extensive: they depend on population size, so a count map largely shows where people live. Crude rates are intensive: dividing by the population at risk shows risk. A city can have the most cases but an average rate; a small rural area can have few cases but a high rate.









NoteW9. [instructor] Why are estimates from areas with small populations unstable, and how does Empirical Bayes smoothing respond?





The variance of a crude risk is π(1 − π)/P, so small P gives large variance: rates far from the truth in both directions by chance. EB smoothing replaces each rate with a weighted average of the area’s crude rate and the reference rate, with weight w = σ²/(σ² + μ/P). Small areas get small w (strong shrinkage toward the reference), large areas keep their own rate.









NoteW10. [instructor] Is the reference rate π̂ the average of all area rates? What does SMR > 1 mean?





No: π̂ = total events / total population, a population-weighted average. The simple mean of area rates weights every area equally and can be pulled by small areas with extreme rates. SMR > 1 means more events than expected if the reference rate applied in that area (SMR = 1.4: 40% more than expected), but on its own it is not evidence of real excess risk.









NoteW11. [instructor] Describe three ways of defining spatial neighbours and one weakness of each.





Contiguity (rook: shared edge; queen: edge or corner): islands get no neighbours, and neighbour counts vary. Distance band (all within a critical distance): dense areas get very many neighbours, sparse areas few or none unless the threshold is large. k-nearest neighbours: everyone has exactly k neighbours and no isolates, but the matrix is asymmetric and ties must be handled.









NoteW12. [instructor] Explain the basic idea of Moran’s I and how its significance is assessed.





Moran’s I is a cross-product statistic: it sums zᵢzⱼ (deviations from the mean) over neighbouring pairs, scaled by the variance, so it behaves like a correlation between a variable and its spatial lag. Positive: similar values cluster; negative: dissimilar values are neighbours; near 0 (exactly −1/(n−1)): spatial randomness. Significance: compare the observed I with a reference distribution under spatial randomness, either analytically (normal approximation) or by random permutations of the values over the areas (pseudo p-value).









NoteW13. [instructor] Distinguish global from local spatial autocorrelation. What does a LISA cluster map show?





Global (Moran’s I) gives one number: is there clustering in the whole map? Local (LISA, local Moran’s I) gives a statistic and pseudo p-value per area: where are the clusters and outliers? The cluster map shows significant areas as High-High and Low-Low clusters (positive local autocorrelation) and High-Low and Low-High spatial outliers (negative), relative to the mean. The sum of local Moran’s I values is proportional to the global I.









NoteW14. Interpret positive and negative spatial autocorrelation, with a map description of each.





Positive: neighbouring areas have similar values; on the map, blocks of high values and blocks of low values (like the half-black, half-white grid). Negative: neighbours tend to differ; on the map, a checkerboard. Positive autocorrelation is far more common in health data.





Session 3: spatial regression






NoteW15. Why can spatial dependence be a problem in an OLS regression of area-level data?





OLS assumes no remaining dependence in the errors after accounting for X. If residuals are spatially autocorrelated, neighbouring areas carry overlapping information, so OLS standard errors are typically too small (p-values too small), and if the dependence comes from a spatial process in the outcome or a spatially patterned omitted variable, the coefficients can also be biased.









NoteW16. Compare the spatial lag (SAR) and spatial error (SEM) models: equation, mechanism, interpretation of the spatial parameter.





SAR: y = ρWy + Xβ + ε. Dependence enters through the outcome; ρ is how strongly an area’s outcome is linked to its neighbours’ outcomes; mechanisms are interaction, diffusion, feedback (infectious disease). SEM: y = Xβ + u, u = λWu + ε. Dependence is in the error; λ is how spatially structured the unexplained part is; mechanisms are omitted spatially patterned determinants (poorly measured air quality). Same symptom (autocorrelated OLS residuals), different story.









NoteW17. In a SAR model, why should you report direct, indirect and total impacts instead of β?





Because y appears on both sides, a change in x in one area changes its y, which spreads to neighbours and feeds back: y = (I − ρW)⁻¹(Xβ + ε). The direct impact (own area, including feedback) is larger than β when ρ > 0, the indirect impact is the spillover to other areas, and with row-standardized W the total is β/(1 − ρ). Reporting only β understates the effect.









NoteW18. [instructor] After adjusting for covariates, neighbouring areas still have similar residuals. What could that mean, and how would you proceed?





A spatial process linking outcomes (SAR), an omitted spatially patterned determinant (SEM), or something else: misspecification or spatial heterogeneity. Proceed: map residuals and test residual Moran’s I; ask which mechanism is plausible for this outcome; compare SAR and SEM with LM tests (robust versions if both simple tests are significant) and check residuals again; interpret carefully (impacts for SAR, no causal language without a causal design). Diagnostics support reasoning, they do not replace it.









NoteW19. [instructor] Scenario: neighbouring municipalities share an incompletely measured air-quality environment. Which model is the natural starting point, and why? What about an infectious outcome diffusing between connected municipalities?





Air quality: SEM, because the dependence comes from an unmeasured, spatially smooth exposure, so the errors are correlated. Infectious diffusion: SAR may be plausible, because outcomes in one area directly affect outcomes in connected areas. The point is to articulate the assumed process.





Session 4: Bayesian disease mapping






NoteW20. [instructor] Why might two areas with the same SMR provide very different amounts of information about their underlying risk?





The SMR is a ratio and hides the size of the counts. Area A with 3 observed and 1 expected and area B with 300 and 100 both have SMR = 3, but the standard error is roughly SMR/√Y: about 1.7 for A and 0.17 for B. A few chance cases change A’s SMR enormously, so A’s data are compatible with a wide range of true risks.









NoteW21. [instructor] How do the epidemiological outcome and denominator determine the likelihood?





Incidence or mortality (events over person-time): Poisson with log person-time as offset, target the rate. Prevalence (cases among N examined, each yes/no): Binomial(N, p), target the probability. Observed versus expected counts: Poisson(Eθ), target the relative risk. A count is not automatically Poisson; BYM2 can be added to either likelihood.









NoteW22. [instructor] Explain shrinkage, partial pooling and spatial smoothing.





Partial pooling: area estimates are drawn from a shared distribution, so each is a compromise between its own data and the common pattern. Shrinkage is the result: noisy estimates move toward the common pattern, more for data-poor areas, less for data-rich ones. Spatial smoothing is partial pooling where the common pattern is local: a CAR/ICAR prior centres each area’s effect on its neighbours’ effects.









NoteW23. [instructor] What is the difference between partial pooling and spatial smoothing?





Unstructured partial pooling shrinks every area toward the same global mean and ignores the map (shuffling the areas changes nothing). Spatial smoothing shrinks each area toward the mean of its neighbours, using the adjacency graph. Spatial smoothing is a geographic form of partial pooling.









NoteW24. [instructor] Why does the BYM2 model include both spatially structured and unstructured variation?





Because not all residual variation is spatial. The structured component uᵢ captures smooth, clustered patterns; the unstructured vᵢ allows area-specific departures that need not resemble neighbours. Without vᵢ, all residual differences are forced into the spatial surface (over-smoothing); without uᵢ, geography is ignored. The mixing parameter ρ lets the data decide the balance, and τ controls the overall amount.









NoteW25. [instructor] If ρ in BYM2 is estimated at 0.9, does that mean 90% of disease cases are caused by spatial factors?





No. ρ is the fraction of the residual (unexplained) latent between-area variation that is spatially structured, on the BYM2 mixing scale. It says nothing about causes or cases, and nothing about the variation explained by covariates.









NoteW26. [instructor] Interpret a posterior 95% credible interval for a relative risk of [1.08, 1.42], and contrast it with a confidence interval.





Under the fitted model and priors, there is 95% posterior probability that the area’s latent relative risk lies between 1.08 and 1.42: a probability statement about the parameter, conditional on model, data and priors. A 95% confidence interval instead means that 95% of intervals constructed this way in repeated samples would contain the fixed true value.









NoteW27. [instructor] Why might an area with a higher estimated relative risk have weaker evidence of elevated risk than another area?





Magnitude and certainty differ. An area with few expected cases has a wide posterior: its mean can be high (1.30) while its credible interval includes 1 and P(RR > 1) is only 0.72. A large area can have a smaller but precise excess (1.20, CrI 1.10–1.31, P(RR > 1) = 0.995), which is stronger evidence. Exceedance probabilities make this visible.









NoteW28. Give two reasons to be cautious when interpreting a smoothed disease map.





Smoothing can hide real boundaries (a river, catchment or policy border) and attenuate sharp local signals, so the adjacency definition is a substantive choice. And a high posterior risk is not a causal explanation: ecological inference, spatial confounding between covariates and the spatial effect, and the MAUP all limit what can be concluded.





Session 5: the computer lab






NoteW29. An area has posterior mean RR = 1.6 and P(RR > 1) = 0.70; another has RR = 1.15 and P(RR > 1) = 0.97. Classify both with the 0.8 rule and explain.





The first is “uncertain” (0.70 is between 0.2 and 0.8): its estimated excess is large, but its posterior is wide, typically because the expected count is small. The second is “elevated” (0.97 > 0.8): a modest excess estimated precisely. The rule classifies by certainty, not size; the posterior RR and its credible interval give the size. The rule is conservative: moderate real excesses in small areas are often left as “uncertain”.









NoteW30. OLS residuals had a significant Moran’s I. After fitting a spatial error model, residual Moran’s I was close to zero. What does this show, and what does it not show?





It shows that the spatial dependence in the residuals has been absorbed by the error process u = λWu + ε, so inference on β is no longer based on falsely independent errors. It does not show that SEM is the true mechanism: a SAR model might remove the residual autocorrelation too. The choice between lag and error should rest on the substantive story (diffusion and feedback vs omitted spatially patterned determinants), supported by LM tests.





Session 6: additional methods and applications






NoteW31. [instructor] Describe how ESDA can help identify spatial patterns and spatial heterogeneity.





ESDA links non-spatial graphs with a map: selecting in a histogram, box plot or scatter plot highlights the same areas on the map, and brushing the map updates the graphs. This shows whether extreme values cluster and where. Heterogeneity is examined by comparing spatially selected areas with the rest: the averages chart tests for a difference in means (F = t² with two groups), and brushing a scatter plot fits separate regression lines whose slopes can be compared with a Chow test. LOWESS fits can reveal nonlinearity or a structural break. ESDA generates hypotheses; its simple tests ignore heteroskedasticity and spatial autocorrelation, so confirmatory analysis needs, for example, spatial regime models.









NoteW32. [instructor] Which of two LOWESS curves comes from the larger bandwidth, and why?





The smoother one. The bandwidth is the fraction of the x-range used in each local fit; a larger bandwidth averages over more observations, so local slopes change slowly. A small bandwidth gives a jagged curve that follows noise; a too-large one can hide a real bend.









NoteW33. [instructor] Compare container, minimum-distance and floating catchment area measures of spatial accessibility, and give one limitation of each.





Container: counts facilities inside an area (point-in-polygon) or within buffers. Limitation: depends on the boundaries and buffer size and ignores services just across the border. Minimum distance: distance to the nearest facility. Limitation: ignores facility size and how many people compete for it. 2SFCA: for each facility the supply-to-population ratio in its catchment, summed over the facilities reachable from each location. It combines supply, demand and distance, but the catchment size and distance decay are choices that change the result, and it measures potential, not realized, access. All capture only the spatial dimensions of access (availability and accessibility), not affordability, acceptability or accommodation. Different measures can lead to different conclusions about inequity (Talen & Anselin 1998).









NoteW34. [instructor] Explain how PCA and clustering can be used to characterize multidimensional neighbourhood conditions. Use Kolak et al. (2020) as the example.





Neighbourhood conditions are measured by many correlated indicators. PCA replaces them with a few orthogonal components, linear combinations that keep as much variance as possible; Kolak et al. reduced 15 SDOH variables to 4 indices (socioeconomic advantage, limited mobility, urban core opportunity, mixed immigrant cohesion and accessibility) explaining 71% of the variance. The indices can be interpreted, mapped and tested for clusters with LISA. K-means on the indices, with tract centroids added for spatial proximity, grouped tracts into seven neighbourhood typologies. The indices can then be used in spatial regression (Lin et al. 2022), avoiding collinearity among the original variables.









NoteW35. How does K-means work, and how can it be made spatial? How do you choose K?





K-means assigns every observation to exactly one of K clusters, measures dissimilarity by squared Euclidean distance over the variables, and iteratively relocates observations (assign to the nearest centre, recompute the centres) to minimize within-cluster dissimilarity. It ignores location, so clusters can be scattered; it is made spatial by adding centroid coordinates as extra variables or by weighting attribute similarity against geographic co-location. K is chosen with an elbow plot of the within-cluster sum of squares against K: WCSS always falls, so pick the K after which it falls much more slowly, also considering interpretability.









NoteW36. [instructor] Distinguish spatial association from causal inference. Name three challenges specific to spatial data.





A spatial association (from a map or a spatial regression) says that health and an area characteristic go together; a causal question asks what would happen if we intervened. Three challenges: spatial dependence (nearby outcomes or errors are correlated), spatially structured confounding (geographic factors such as deprivation affect both exposure and outcome), and spatial interference (an intervention in one area changes outcomes in another). Spatial dependence is not the same as interference. Spatial models help with dependence; study design supports causality.









NoteW37. [instructor] Does a spatial lag represent a causal spillover?





Not by itself. In SAR, a change in x propagates through (I − ρW)⁻¹, giving model-implied indirect impacts. A causal spillover is how an intervention in area j would change the outcome in area i. The two coincide only if the model is causally correct: the right W, no spatially structured confounding, and dependence that truly runs through the outcomes rather than omitted variables. A causal interpretation needs a credible design and assumptions.









NoteW38. Explain difference-in-differences and its key assumption. Treated: 60 → 51; control: 45 → 42. Estimate the effect.





DiD compares the change in the treated group with the change in the control group, which removes time-invariant differences between the groups and shocks common to both. Effect = (51 − 60) − (42 − 45) = −9 − (−3) = −6. Key assumption: parallel trends, meaning that without the intervention the treated group would have changed as much as the control. This concerns the untreated counterfactual changes, not equal baseline levels; here the groups start at different levels, which is allowed.









NoteW39. [instructor] Can a neighbouring municipality serve as a control when evaluating a geographically targeted intervention?





It is risky. Residents of a neighbouring municipality may cross the border and use the intervention (spatial interference), so the neighbour is partly treated. Its change then includes some of the benefit, and DiD underestimates the effect (biased toward zero). A distant municipality is plausibly unexposed but may be less comparable (different trends). Options: define a spatial treatment exposure Gᵢ = Σⱼ wᵢⱼDⱼ and select controls with no exposure, exclude a buffer zone around treated areas, or model the spillover explicitly.









NoteW40. [instructor] Match each research question to a method. (a) Where are the hot spots of childhood asthma? (b) Is neighbourhood deprivation associated with asthma, accounting for spatial dependence? (c) Did a low-emission zone introduced in one city reduce asthma admissions?






Where? Describe: LISA, or Bayesian disease mapping with exceedance probabilities for unstable small-area rates. (b) Associated with what? Spatial regression (SAR or SEM, chosen by mechanism), possibly with regimes for heterogeneity. (c) What if we intervene? A causal design: DiD comparing the city’s change with comparable cities without a zone (parallel trends), or geographic RDD at the zone boundary, with attention to spillover to neighbouring areas and to why the city introduced the zone.






Session 7: guest lecture






NoteW41. How can disease mapping help identify geographic inequalities in cancer detection, and why is evaluating a targeted intervention harder than identifying target areas?





Mapping stage at diagnosis or screening participation by small area, with Bayesian smoothing and exceedance probabilities, shows where detection is reliably worse rather than where small counts happen to be extreme; socioeconomic covariates or indices show whether the gaps follow deprivation. Evaluation is harder because it is causal: target areas were chosen for being worse (confounding, regression to the mean), so a before–after look is not enough. A design with comparable control areas, such as DiD, is needed, with parallel trends and possible spillover to neighbouring areas in mind.
