title: Session 1 — Introduction to Spatial Epidemiology
text:
This first session sets up the vocabulary for the whole course. It answers three questions: what makes data spatial, what spatial epidemiology is trying to achieve, and which problems are special to analysing health data by place.
The thread running through the session, and the rest of the course, is a sentence from the last slide: a map is often the beginning of the epidemiologic question, not the end. Seeing where disease is high leads to asking why it is high there, and then what can be done.
The second half introduces the methodological issues that come back in every later session: the modifiable areal unit problem (MAUP), the ecological fallacy, spatial dependence and spatial heterogeneity.

title: Session 1 — Introduction to Spatial Epidemiology
section: 1.1 What is spatial data?
text:
1.1 What is spatial data?

In short. Spatial data are ordinary data with a location attached. The location is stored either as exact shapes (vector: points, lines, polygons) or as a grid of cells (raster). Most of this course uses polygons: areas such as municipalities, each with a count or a rate.

Spatial data = information + location. The information (an attribute: a disease rate, an income, a pollution level) is tied to a place. The information may change with location; that is the point of studying it spatially. Very occasionally spatial data contain only location (a list of clinic coordinates), but without location the data are no longer spatial.
A spatial data file has two parts that belong together:

the geometry: where each feature is (coordinates, or the outline of an area);
the attribute table: one row per feature with its variables, like an ordinary data frame.

Two ways of representing space









Model
How space is stored
Feature types
Typical health example




Vector
Exact coordinates of points and the vertices that join them
Point (one coordinate pair), line (connected points), polygon / area (closed line)
Case addresses (points), roads (lines), municipalities or DeSO areas (polygons)


Raster
A grid of equal cells; every cell holds a value
The same shapes, approximated by filled cells
Air-pollution surfaces, land cover, satellite temperature











Figure 1: The three feature types in the two data models (after slide 5). Vector data store exact coordinates; raster data approximate the same shapes with filled grid cells.





In the lecture notes, area = polygon. Most of this course works with areal (polygon) data: counts or rates aggregated to administrative areas.

  Vector points for homes and a raster grid for pollution
  Vector polygons for homes and vector lines for pollution
  A raster grid for homes and vector points for pollution
  Two raster grids at different cell sizes for both layers
  A home address is a single coordinate pair, a vector point. A pollution surface measured on 1 km cells is a raster. Joining them means looking up the cell value at each point.


On the exam, be able to say: Spatial data = information + location. Vector data store points, lines and polygons as coordinates; raster data store values in a regular grid of cells.

title: Session 1 — Introduction to Spatial Epidemiology
section: 1.2 Spatial file formats: CSV, shapefile, GeoJSON
text:
1.2 Spatial file formats: CSV, shapefile, GeoJSON

In short. A spatial file has to carry three things: the shapes, the data table and the coordinate system. A shapefile splits them over at least four files that must stay together; GeoJSON keeps everything in one file; a CSV works only for points with coordinate columns.









Format
What it is
Watch out for




CSV (or other text file)
An ordinary table. It is spatial only if it has coordinate columns (longitude, latitude)
Cannot store polygons in a practical way; the CRS is not recorded in the file


Shapefile
ESRI’s format. At least four files with the same name and different extensions
All files must sit in the same folder; if one is missing the layer breaks


GeoJSON
Open standard text format for points, lines and polygons with attributes
Can be large for detailed boundaries



The four shapefile parts (as written down in class):







Extension
Holds




.shp
The geometry: the shapes themselves


.shx
The index that lets software find each shape quickly


.dbf
The attribute table (one row per shape)


.prj
The projection: which coordinate reference system the coordinates are in




“The .shp file is the shapefile, so I only need to send that.” The .shp holds the shapes but no attributes and no CRS. Without .dbf you lose the data columns, and without .prj the software does not know where on Earth the coordinates belong. Keep all parts together.


  The .prj file, so the coordinate reference system is unknown
  The .dbf file, so the attribute columns cannot be read
  The .shx file, so the shapes cannot be indexed at all
  A GeoJSON copy, which shapefiles need for their geometry
  Shapes and attributes load fine (.shp, .shx, .dbf are there). What is missing is the projection information in .prj: without it, software cannot place or transform the coordinates correctly.


On the exam, be able to say: A shapefile has at least four parts in the same folder: .shp (geometry), .shx (index), .dbf (attribute table) and .prj (projection/CRS).

title: Session 1 — Introduction to Spatial Epidemiology
section: 1.3 Coordinate reference systems and EPSG codes
text:
1.3 Coordinate reference systems and EPSG codes

In short. Coordinates mean nothing without a coordinate reference system (CRS): it says where on Earth the numbers point and how the round Earth was flattened. Put all layers in the same CRS before combining them, and use a CRS in metres for distances.
Think of it as: Currencies. “100” means nothing until you know whether it is kronor or euros, and you must convert before you add two amounts.

The Earth is round; a map is flat. A coordinate reference system (CRS) says how coordinates relate to places on the Earth’s surface, and for a projected CRS, which method was used to flatten (project) the surface onto two dimensions. Different projections give visibly different world maps: every projection distorts area, shape, distance or direction somehow.
CRSs are identified by EPSG codes (from the European Petroleum Survey Group): a standard number that pins down the datum, the coordinate system and the projection.









EPSG:4326 (WGS 84)
EPSG:3006 (SWEREF 99 TM)




Kind
Geographic (unprojected)
Projected


Coordinates
Longitude and latitude
Easting and northing


Units
Degrees
Metres


Typical use
GPS, web maps, data downloaded online
Swedish national spatial data


Distances and areas
Not directly: a degree of longitude shrinks towards the poles
Yes, Euclidean distance in metres is meaningful



Two practical rules from the slides:

Recognise 4326. Coordinates like 41.784766, -87.609299 (small numbers with many decimals, within ±90 and ±180) are almost certainly longitude/latitude in EPSG:4326. Try that first.
Transform before you join. When you combine layers, put everything in the same CRS first. Layers in different CRSs will not line up, and spatial joins or distances will be wrong.

For distance or area calculations, transform to a suitable projected CRS (in Sweden, SWEREF 99 TM). This returns in Session 2: Euclidean distance between points is only meaningful for projected coordinates.

  Transform the points to a projected CRS in metres, such as SWEREF 99 TM
  Use a 5-degree distance band, because the coordinates are in degrees
  Nothing, since Euclidean distance works the same in any CRS
  Convert the shapefile to GeoJSON, which stores distances in metres
  In EPSG:4326, coordinates are in degrees, and one degree is not a fixed number of metres. A 5 km threshold needs projected coordinates in metres (or great-circle distances). File format does not change the CRS.


On the exam, be able to say: A CRS defines how coordinates relate to the Earth’s surface; EPSG codes identify it. EPSG:4326 (WGS 84) is in degrees; projected systems such as SWEREF 99 TM (EPSG:3006) are in metres and are needed for distances and areas. Layers must share a CRS before they are joined.

title: Session 1 — Introduction to Spatial Epidemiology
section: 1.4 Geocoding and Swedish small areas (DeSO)
text:
1.4 Geocoding and Swedish small areas (DeSO)

In short. Geocoding turns an address into coordinates. Health data are usually reported for administrative areas; in Sweden the smallest standard unit is DeSO.

Geocoding turns an address into coordinates (longitude and latitude), so that individuals can be placed on a map or linked to the area they live in. Geocoding can fail or be wrong (missing or misspelled addresses, rural addresses placed at a postcode centroid). Such errors are rarely random: they are more common in some kinds of areas, which can bias a spatial analysis (see 1.13).
Most health data are reported for administrative areas: province, county, postcode, census tract. In Sweden the smallest standard statistical unit is DeSO (demografiska statistikområden, demographic statistical areas), designed by Statistics Sweden to have roughly 700 to 2,700 inhabitants each, so that statistics can be published at fine scale without identifying people. The lecture notes record DeSO as the smallest area in Sweden used in practice.
Why the choice of unit matters is the subject of 1.10 Scale and MAUP.

On the exam, be able to say: Geocoding converts addresses to longitude/latitude; failures are often concentrated in some areas, so they are not random. DeSO are Sweden’s small statistical areas of roughly 700–2,700 inhabitants.

title: Session 1 — Introduction to Spatial Epidemiology
section: 1.5 John Snow and the 1854 cholera outbreak
text:
1.5 John Snow and the 1854 cholera outbreak

In short. In London in 1854, John Snow mapped cholera deaths and water pumps. Deaths clustered around one pump, and comparing households with different water supplies supported his idea that cholera spreads through water, not “bad air”.

The in-class activity: read the story map (about 15 minutes) and answer three questions.







Question
Answer




Research question
What causes cholera, and why did so many people in one part of Soho, London, die in a few days in 1854?


Competing hypotheses
Miasma: disease spreads through “bad air” from rotting matter (the dominant view). Waterborne: cholera is transmitted through contaminated water (Snow’s hypothesis)


Spatial data used
The locations of cholera deaths (point data, stacked as bars at each house) and the locations of public water pumps on a street map. Snow also compared deaths by which water company supplied a household



The map showed deaths clustered around the Broad Street pump. Exceptions were informative: workers at a brewery with its own water supply were largely spared, while some deaths far away were in people who preferred to fetch water from Broad Street. The pump handle was removed.
Classifying Snow’s work with the describe–analyze–intervene framework (1.7): mapping the deaths describes; testing the water hypothesis against miasma (including the comparison of water companies) analyzes; removing the pump handle is an intervention. One study can move across all three goals, which is exactly what modern spatial epidemiology rarely does.

“Snow’s map proved the cause.” The map alone shows clustering around a pump, which miasma could also explain (bad air near the pump). What made the argument strong was theory (a waterborne mechanism), informative exceptions, and a comparison between households with different water supply. A map starts the question; the comparison answers it.


On the exam, be able to say: Research question: what caused the outbreak and how cholera spreads. Competing hypotheses: miasma (bad air) vs contaminated water. Data: death locations (points), pump locations and water supply by household. Snow described, analysed and intervened (the pump handle).

title: Session 1 — Introduction to Spatial Epidemiology
section: 1.6 Definitions of spatial epidemiology
text:
1.6 Definitions of spatial epidemiology

In short. Spatial epidemiology studies how disease varies between places, and why. The newer, broader definition adds that the aim is also to act: to inform interventions that improve health.

Three definitions from the slides, from narrow to broad:



Source
Definition (key words)




Elliott & Wartenberg (2004)
“the description and analysis of geographic variations in disease with respect to demographic, environmental, behavioral, socioeconomic, genetic, and infectious risk factors”


Lawson (2018)
uses geographic location to understand the distribution of health outcomes and their determinants, considering how location influences the interaction of risk factors


Morrison et al. (2024), broader
applies theory and methods from epidemiology, geography and statistics to describe spatial distributions, analyze possible causes, inform intervention, and improve health



The lecture notes record the first definition: geographic variations in disease with respect to demographic and other risk factors. Be able to reproduce one definition in your own words and say what the broader one adds: an explicit aim to explain and to intervene, not just to map.

On the exam, be able to say: Spatial epidemiology is the description and analysis of geographic variation in disease with respect to demographic, environmental, behavioural, socioeconomic, genetic and infectious risk factors. Morrison et al. broaden it to describe, analyse and intervene.

title: Session 1 — Introduction to Spatial Epidemiology
section: 1.7 Describe → analyze → intervene (Morrison et al. 2024)
text:
1.7 Describe → analyze → intervene (Morrison et al. 2024)

In short. A study can describe (where is disease?), analyse (why there?) or intervene (what can we change?). A large review found many descriptive and analytic studies but no intervention studies.
Think of it as: A doctor who is excellent at diagnosis and at explaining the illness, but never tests a treatment.

Morrison et al. (2024, Epidemiology 35(4):542–555) reviewed the spatial epidemiology literature and asked whether the field is aligned with the broader goals of epidemiology.





flowchart LR
  D["DESCRIBE<br/>Where is health distributed?<br/>(disease mapping, cluster detection,<br/>surveillance, resource allocation)"] --> A["ANALYZE<br/>Why might the pattern occur?<br/>(place-based determinants,<br/>exposure–outcome relationships,<br/>mechanisms, inequalities)"]
  A --> I["INTERVENE<br/>What can we change?<br/>(target interventions, evaluate<br/>place-based policies,<br/>change environments)"]


 Workflow: each arrow means “then”, the next goal a study can move on to. Not causal. The three goals of epidemiology as used in Morrison et al. (2024). 



What the review found among 482 papers:



Type
Number




Descriptive
122


Analytic
167


Intervention
0


Reviews
76


Demonstrations of methods
117



Zero intervention studies. The field is good at mapping patterns and developing methods, but mainly describes and explains; it rarely evaluates what works. The slides’ re-orientation: spatial statistical methods are tools, not the endpoint. The question is not only “Where are the clusters?” but “Why are they there, and what can we do about them?”
From where to why requires more than a map: pattern → theory → analysis. Theory tells you which spatial units, exposures, pathways, confounders and mechanisms are meaningful.

On the exam, be able to say: Morrison et al. (2024) classified 482 papers: 122 descriptive, 167 analytic, 0 intervention. Spatial methods are tools, not the endpoint: the field should move from where to why to what can be done.

title: Session 1 — Introduction to Spatial Epidemiology
section: 1.8 Why place matters for health
text:
1.8 Why place matters for health

In short. Where people live shapes what they are exposed to (air, noise, food) and what they can reach (care, parks, schools). That is why place itself is studied as a determinant of health.

Physical and social environments produce health disparities. Examples from the slides:

longer distance to mammography facilities → later breast cancer diagnosis (Nattinger 2001; note: the paper itself studies distance to a radiotherapy facility and the choice of breast cancer surgery);
pedestrian-friendly environments → lower obesity (Gordon-Larsen 2006);
living along major traffic corridors → cardiovascular disease (McEntee 2008; note: the paper itself studies diesel particulate matter, lung cancer and asthma along traffic corridors).

Three frameworks that put place inside epidemiology:



Framework
Core idea




Social determinants of health (WHO 2010)
The conditions in which people are born, grow, live, work and age, including neighbourhood and physical environment and access to healthcare, shape health


Eco-epidemiology (Schwartz et al. 1999)
Individuals are interdependent and connected to the biological, physical, social and historical contexts they live in


Multiple exposures over the life span (Buck Louis & Sundaram 2012)
Measure many environmental exposures at different times in life, not one exposure at one time



The common message: place stands for context: access to food, care, education, green space and clean air.

On the exam, be able to say: Physical and social environments produce health disparities (for example distance to care, walkability, traffic exposure). Frameworks: social determinants of health, eco-epidemiology, multiple exposures across the life span.

title: Session 1 — Introduction to Spatial Epidemiology
section: 1.9 Theoretical frameworks: social-ecological model and life course
text:
1.9 Theoretical frameworks: social-ecological model and life course

In short. Two ways to organise the causes of health. The social-ecological model places the individual inside nested levels (relationships, organisations, community). The life-course model describes five steps through which social position becomes unequal health. Spatial data fit at the neighbourhood level.

Both frameworks were written down in class.
Social-ecological model (Bronfenbrenner 1994; Dahlberg & Krug 2002). Health is shaped by nested levels:







Level
Example from the slide (stigma around opioid use disorder)




Individual
Age, race/ethnicity, education


Interpersonal
Friends’ or family members’ experience with the disorder


Organizational
Workplaces, clinics, schools


Community / neighbourhood
Spatial access to treatment (medication for opioid use disorder)



Spatial data enter at the outer level: the neighbourhood and what is reachable from it.
Life-course perspective: five mechanisms behind social inequality in health (Diderichsen et al. 2001):









Mechanism
Where spatial data can help




I
Social stratification: people end up in different social positions
Residential segregation by income


II
Differential exposure: lower positions meet more causes of illness
Pollution, noise, unhealthy food environments by area


III
Differential vulnerability: the same exposure harms some groups more
Area deprivation modifying the effect of heat


IV
Differential disease consequences: illness leads to worse outcomes for some
Distance to care, late diagnosis


V
Consequences for the individual and society: illness feeds back into social position
Job loss concentrated in some areas



The in-class discussion question was where spatial data and spatial epidemiology may be useful, and how. A good answer links one mechanism to one spatial measure, as in the right-hand column.

On the exam, be able to say: Social-ecological model: individual, interpersonal, organisational and community levels. Diderichsen’s five mechanisms: social stratification, differential exposure, differential vulnerability, differential consequences, and consequences for the individual and society.

title: Session 1 — Introduction to Spatial Epidemiology
section: 1.10 Scale and the modifiable areal unit problem (MAUP)
text:
1.10 Scale and the modifiable areal unit problem (MAUP)

In short. Results from area data depend on which areas you use. Make the areas bigger, or draw the borders differently, and the map and the statistics can change, even though the people are the same.
Think of it as: Average grades by class, by school or by municipality: each level tells a different story about the same pupils.

Health data are usually aggregated to administrative zones (province, county, postcode, census tract, DeSO). These units:

are often irregular and arbitrary, drawn for administration, not for health;
can change over time (inconsistent geography), which makes trends hard to follow.

The modifiable areal unit problem (MAUP) (Openshaw 1984): changing the spatial units can lead to different statistical results and interpretations, even when the underlying individual data are the same. The lecture notes put it as: if we change scale (new areas are under investigation), the interpretation will change.
MAUP has two parts:








Effect
What changes
Example




Scale effect
The size of the units (DeSO → municipality → county)
A correlation between deprivation and mortality gets stronger as units get larger, because aggregation averages out individual noise


Zoning effect
Where the boundaries are drawn, at the same size
Two ways of drawing 20 equal-sized districts give different cluster maps











Figure 2: Zoning effect, simulated. The same 64 small units, with high values along a diagonal band, aggregated into four zones in three different ways. Vertical or horizontal strips hide the band almost completely; squares turn it into two ‘hot’ and two ‘cold’ quarters. Same data, three different maps.





A partial remedy from the slides: a regular hexagon grid (all units the same size and shape), but health data are rarely available on such grids.





Scale effect, simulated. The same 3,600 individuals (exposure x and outcome y with a weak individual-level association, plus a smooth spatial trend in both) are aggregated to 900, 36 and 9 areas. The correlation of the area means grows as the areas get larger.




The individual-level correlation in this simulation is about 0.25. None of the area-level correlations is “the” answer: each describes associations between areas at that scale.






TipWhen to use this idea



Whenever results come from aggregated data: say which unit was used, ask whether conclusions hold at another scale, and prefer units that make sense for the mechanism (a health-care catchment for access to care, a smaller unit for air pollution).



On the exam, be able to say: MAUP: changing the spatial units (scale effect: their size; zoning effect: where the borders go) can change results and interpretations even though the underlying data are the same.

title: Session 1 — Introduction to Spatial Epidemiology
section: 1.11 The ecological fallacy
text:
1.11 The ecological fallacy

In short. A pattern between areas does not have to hold for the individuals in them.
Think of it as: A neighbourhood with high income and many votes for one party does not prove that the rich residents voted for that party.

Ecological fallacy (Robinson 1950): drawing incorrect inferences about individuals from group-level data.
Example from the slides: a region has a high crime rate, so one concludes that an individual from that region is likely to commit a crime. The aggregate does not describe individual characteristics or behaviour.








Figure 3: Ecological fallacy, simulated. Left: across three areas, higher average exposure goes with a higher average outcome. Right: within every area, individuals with higher exposure have a lower outcome. The area-level association says nothing reliable about individuals.





MAUP vs ecological fallacy. Both come from aggregation, but they ask different things:









MAUP
Ecological fallacy




The problem
Area-level results depend on how the areas are drawn
Area-level results are wrongly applied to individuals


Level of the conclusion
Stays at area level
Jumps from area to individual level


Question it raises
Would I see the same pattern with other units?
Does this association hold for people?




  The ecological fallacy: an area association is applied to individuals
  The modifiable areal unit problem: the boundaries were drawn badly
  Spatial heterogeneity: the association differs between regions
  Geocoding error: outlets were placed in the wrong municipality
  The data are at municipality level. Whether the individuals with diabetes ate fast food is not observed; inferring it is the ecological fallacy. MAUP would be the issue if the conclusion were about municipalities but changed with other boundaries.


On the exam, be able to say: The ecological fallacy is drawing conclusions about individuals from group-level data. It differs from the MAUP, which is about area-level results changing with the choice of areas.

title: Session 1 — Introduction to Spatial Epidemiology
section: 1.12 Spatial dependence and spatial heterogeneity
text:
1.12 Spatial dependence and spatial heterogeneity

In short. Dependence: neighbours tend to be alike. Heterogeneity: the rules themselves change from place to place.
Think of it as: Dependence: houses on the same street have similar prices. Heterogeneity: an extra room adds more to the price in Stockholm than in a small town.

These are the two properties that make spatial data special, and they motivate every method in the rest of the course.
Spatial dependence. Tobler’s first law of geography: “things closer together are more similar than things further apart”. Observations near one another may be more similar (or otherwise related) than observations far apart. Example: expensive and cheap neighbourhoods cluster because of socio-spatial processes. Dependence usually holds within some distance; beyond it, observations behave as independent.
Global measures summarise dependence in one number:







Measure
Reading




Moran’s I ≈ 0
Little or no global spatial autocorrelation


Moran’s I > 0
Similar values tend to occur near one another (clustering)


Moran’s I < 0
Dissimilar values tend to occur near one another (checkerboard)


Geary’s C
An alternative global measure (built on squared differences between neighbours)



Both can be tested for statistical significance; Session 2 shows how.
Spatial heterogeneity. Processes and relationships differ by location, so one model applied everywhere can miss local patterns. Example: the relationship between income and housing prices differs between urban and rural areas. It shows up as regression coefficients that vary across regions, or as spatially structured random effects (Session 4).









Spatial dependence
Spatial heterogeneity




About
Similarity between nearby values
Differences in processes or relationships across space


Question
Are neighbours alike?
Is the same model valid everywhere?


Methods in this course
Moran’s I, LISA (S2); spatial lag and error models (S3); structured random effects (S4)
Mentioned; GWR and similar models are outside the course (S3)




  Spatial heterogeneity: the relationship differs by location
  Spatial dependence: neighbouring admission counts are similar
  The ecological fallacy: area data are applied to individuals
  The MAUP: the result depends on the boundaries used
  A relationship (temperature → admissions) that changes across space is heterogeneity. Dependence would be about values in neighbouring areas resembling each other, which can be present at the same time but is a different property.


On the exam, be able to say: Spatial dependence (Tobler’s first law): nearby observations are more similar than distant ones; measured by Moran’s I. Spatial heterogeneity: processes or relationships differ by location, so one global model can miss local patterns.

title: Session 1 — Introduction to Spatial Epidemiology
section: 1.13 Other issues: reporting, geocoding, boundaries, sparse counts
text:
1.13 Other issues: reporting, geocoding, boundaries, sparse counts

In short. A map can show the data system instead of the disease: missed reports, failed geocoding, changing borders and tiny populations all create patterns that are not real.

The slides list four further problems. Each is a form of bias in spatial data (the course syllabus asks you to reflect on bias from aggregation, measurement and missing data):







Issue
Why it can bias a map or model




Incomplete or geographically varying reporting
If some regions report less completely, they look healthier than they are. The map shows the reporting system, not the disease


Geocoding failure or error
Failed addresses are dropped or misplaced; failures are often concentrated in rural or new areas (missing data that are not missing at random)


Boundary changes over time
Areas merge or split, so rates before and after are not comparable (inconsistent geography)


Differences in population size / sparse counts
Small areas give unstable rates: extreme values may be chance, not risk. Session 2 (smoothing) and Session 4 (Bayesian disease mapping) deal with this




On the exam, be able to say: Sources of bias: geographically varying reporting, geocoding failures (missing not at random), boundary changes over time, and unstable rates from small populations.

text:
1.14 Tools: GIS, R and GeoDa

In short. GIS is the toolbox for storing, linking, mapping and analysing data by location. The course uses R and GeoDa.

GIS (geographic information systems) and related geospatial methods made spatial epidemiology practical: storing, linking, mapping and analysing data by location. Researchers use R, Stata, ArcGIS, GeoDa, Python and others.
In STA530:

R: the main environment for spatial data analysis and modelling. Useful resources: Geocomputation with R, Spatial Data Science with R and the CSDS R spatial tutorials.
GeoDa: free software for exploratory spatial data analysis and visualisation (maps, weights, Moran’s I, LISA). Install before 13 October (download GeoDa).

The exam tests concepts, not software.

title: Session 1 — Introduction to Spatial Epidemiology
section: 1.15 Session summary and key questions
text:
1.15 Session summary and key questions





flowchart LR
  W["WHERE?<br/>pattern"] --> Y["WHY?<br/>explanation / cause"] --> N["WHAT NEXT?<br/>intervention / action"]


 Lecture map: how the course questions lead into each other. Not causal. 



Why-questions (answer in two or three sentences, then open the model answer):






NoteWhy do you need the .prj file and a known CRS before joining two layers?





Because coordinates are only meaningful relative to a CRS. Two layers in different CRSs describe the same place with different numbers, so they will not overlay, and spatial joins or distance-based neighbours will be wrong. Transform both to the same CRS first, and use a projected CRS in metres for distances.









NoteHow do the MAUP and the ecological fallacy differ, given that both come from aggregation?





The MAUP is about area-level results changing when the areas are redrawn (different size or zoning), even with the same individuals. The ecological fallacy is about wrongly transferring an area-level association to individuals. A result can be robust to the MAUP and still be an ecological fallacy if applied to people.









NoteWhat does “0 intervention studies” in Morrison et al. (2024) say about the field?





Spatial epidemiology has mainly described where disease is and analysed why, and has produced many methods, but has hardly ever evaluated whether place-based actions work. The re-orientation asks studies to go from map (describe) to mechanism (analyze) to action (intervene), as Snow’s work did.









NoteWhy does spatial dependence matter for statistical analysis?





Most standard methods assume independent observations. If nearby areas resemble each other, there is less independent information than the number of areas suggests, and standard errors can be wrong. Dependence can also signal a spatially patterned omitted variable. Sessions 2–4 measure and model it.

title: Session 3 — Introduction to Spatial Regression
text:
Session 2 asked whether nearby values resemble one another. Session 3 asks the regression question: how should a regression model change when observations are spatially dependent?
The starting point is ordinary least squares (OLS). If, after adjusting for covariates, the residuals of neighbouring areas still resemble each other, the model has left something spatial unexplained. There are two classic ways to put spatial dependence into the model, and they tell different scientific stories:
The session’s emphasis is conceptual: what ρ and λ mean, why SAR coefficients cannot be read like OLS coefficients, and how to reason about model choice. No estimator derivations.

title: Session 3 — Introduction to Spatial Regression
section: 3.1 OLS with spatial data: the assumption that can fail
text:
3.1 OLS with spatial data: the assumption that can fail

In short. Ordinary regression assumes that what the model misses (the residuals) is unrelated between observations. With areas, neighbouring residuals are often alike, which makes standard errors too small and can bias the results.

The familiar model:
\[
y = X\beta + \varepsilon .
\]
Key assumption here: after accounting for X, there is no remaining spatial dependence in the errors. Spatial data give a reason to doubt that: the slide shows the same regression equation with two very different residual maps, one that looks random and one with clear clusters of positive and negative residuals.








Figure 1: Two residual maps from the same kind of regression, simulated. Left: residuals scattered at random, residual Moran’s I near 0, the OLS assumption looks fine. Right: positive residuals cluster in some regions and negative in others, residual Moran’s I is high, so something spatial was left out of the model.





Why it matters:

Standard errors. With positively autocorrelated residuals, neighbouring areas carry overlapping information. OLS treats them as independent, so it typically understates the uncertainty: standard errors too small, p-values too small.
Bias. If the spatial pattern comes from a spatial process in the outcome (SAR) or from an omitted spatially patterned confounder, the coefficients themselves can be biased.
Science. Clustered residuals say the model has missed something that is organised in space.


“If I include enough covariates, spatial dependence goes away.” Sometimes, if the covariates capture the spatial process. But clustered residuals can remain after adjustment, and the next step is to ask why (3.2), not to add variables blindly.


On the exam, be able to say: OLS assumes no remaining spatial dependence in the errors after accounting for X. Spatially autocorrelated residuals mean understated uncertainty and possibly biased coefficients.

title: Session 3 — Introduction to Spatial Regression
section: 3.2 After adjustment, neighbouring residuals are similar: what could it mean?
text:
3.2 After adjustment, neighbouring residuals are similar: what could it mean?

In short. If residuals still cluster after adjustment, ask why: outcomes spreading between areas, a missing spatially patterned factor, or a wrongly specified model.

The slide’s example: area-level cardiovascular mortality modelled with age structure, income, smoking prevalence and urbanicity. After adjustment, neighbouring areas still have similar residuals. Possible explanations:









Explanation
Model it points to




A
A spatial process links outcomes across areas (one area’s outcome affects its neighbours’)
Spatial lag (SAR)


B
An omitted determinant is spatially patterned (pollution, access to care, deprivation not fully measured)
Spatial error (SEM)


C
Something else: misspecification (wrong functional form, a missing nonlinear term), spatial heterogeneity (the relationship differs across regions), wrong scale
Fix the model; heterogeneity models (outside the course)



For cardiovascular mortality, A is hard to defend (deaths in one area do not cause deaths next door). B and C are more plausible.

On the exam, be able to say: Three explanations: a spatial process linking outcomes (SAR), an omitted spatially patterned determinant (SEM), or misspecification/heterogeneity.

section: 3.4 The spatial lag model (SAR) and ρ
text:
3.4 The spatial lag model (SAR) and ρ

In short. SAR adds the neighbours’ average outcome as a predictor: y depends on the y next door. ρ says how strongly.
Think of it as: Contagion: an area’s rate rises when its neighbours’ rates rise.

\[
y = \rho W y + X\beta + \varepsilon
\]

In words: an area’s outcome = ρ times its neighbours’ average outcome + the usual covariate part + noise.








Parameter
Meaning




ρ (rho), spatial dependence
How strongly outcomes are linked through W. ρ = 0 gives back OLS; ρ > 0 means an area’s outcome rises with its neighbours’ outcomes


β, covariates
Association with X, conditional on the spatial process


ε, remaining noise
Assumed independent



Key idea: y in one area is jointly determined with y in neighbouring areas. y appears on both sides: that is why OLS cannot simply be applied with Wy as an extra covariate (Wy is correlated with ε; the model is estimated by maximum likelihood or other methods outside the course).
Mechanisms that make SAR plausible: interaction, diffusion, feedback, where the outcome itself spreads.

Optional, from the Canvas post. Luc Anselin’s lecture series Applied Spatial Regression Analysis goes beyond STA530 in places.




On the exam, be able to say: SAR: y = ρWy + Xβ + ε. ρ measures how strongly outcomes are linked through W; y is jointly determined across neighbours.

section: 3.5 Why SAR creates feedback: direct, indirect and total impacts
text:
3.5 Why SAR creates feedback: direct, indirect and total impacts

In short. In SAR, changing x in one area spreads to the neighbours and comes back. So the total effect of x is larger than β and splits into a direct part (own area, including feedback) and an indirect spillover part (other areas).
Think of it as: A stone dropped in a pond: ripples spread outward and bounce back.







NoteDeeper: where the feedback comes from (the Neumann series)





Solve the SAR model for y:
\[
y = (I - \rho W)^{-1} X\beta + (I - \rho W)^{-1}\varepsilon,
\qquad
(I - \rho W)^{-1} = I + \rho W + \rho^2 W^2 + \rho^3 W^3 + \dots
\]
The expansion (the Neumann series, the matrix version of a geometric series) shows how a change spreads:







Term
Path




I
The area’s own effect


ρW
One step: to the neighbours


ρ²W²
Two steps: neighbours of neighbours, including feedback back to the starting area


ρ³W³, …
Continued propagation through the network






Intuition. Raise x in area B. That changes y in B, which (through ρW) changes y in A and C, which feeds back to B, and so on. So β is not the complete impact of x.

Toy example (slide 12). Three areas, everyone neighbours with everyone, ρ = 0.2, β = 1, row-standardized
\[
W = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0.5 & 0.5\\ 0.5 & 0 & 0.5 \\ 0.5 & 0.5 & 0\end{pmatrix}.
\]

The slide shows 1.019 and 0.116; the exact inverse gives 1.023 and 0.114. The total, β/(1 − ρ) = 1/0.8 = 1.25, is the same either way and is the number to remember.








Impact

Direct

Indirect (spillover)

Figure 2: Impacts of raising x by one unit in the centre area (black outline) of a 9 × 9 grid, SAR with β = 1 and row-standardized queen weights. With ρ = 0 only the centre changes (this is OLS). As ρ grows, the change spreads to neighbours and beyond, and feedback raises the centre’s own change (direct impact > 1). The sum of the spillovers can exceed the direct impact.





For SAR, reporting only the raw regression coefficient β can be misleading. Report direct, indirect and total impacts (usually averaged over areas).

title: Session 3 — Introduction to Spatial Regression
section: 3.6 Is a SAR story plausible in epidemiology?
text:
3.6 Is a SAR story plausible in epidemiology?

In short. Choose SAR only if it is plausible that outcomes truly affect each other across borders: infections yes, cancer deaths hardly.

The equation may fit the data; the scientific mechanism still needs to make sense.







Outcome
Genuine cross-area outcome process?




Infectious disease
Plausible: cases in one area contribute to transmission into connected areas


Health behaviours
Plausible: social interaction or diffusion can cross administrative boundaries


Cancer mortality
Hard to defend: neighbouring mortality rates do not “cause” one another. Similar rates nearby more likely reflect shared, partly unmeasured exposures → SEM




On the exam, be able to say: SAR fits a genuine cross-area outcome process (infectious disease, diffusion of behaviours). For outcomes such as cancer mortality the mechanism is implausible; correlated errors (SEM) are a better story.

title: Session 3 — Introduction to Spatial Regression
section: 3.7 The spatial error model (SEM) and λ
text:
3.7 The spatial error model (SEM) and λ

In short. SEM keeps ordinary regression but lets the errors of neighbouring areas be correlated: something unmeasured and spatially smooth is shared. λ says how strongly.
Think of it as: Neighbours who share the same weather: their outcomes are alike, not because they affect each other, but because of a common cause nobody measured.

\[
y = X\beta + u, \qquad u = \lambda W u + \varepsilon
\]

In words: an ordinary regression, except that the error of each area = λ times its neighbours’ errors + fresh noise.








Parameter
Meaning




λ (lambda), error dependence
How strongly the unobserved error process is spatially structured


β, covariates
Regression associations after accounting for correlated errors. Interpreted as in OLS: no spillover impacts


ε, innovation
The remaining independent error



Here neighbouring y values are not on the right-hand side. The dependence sits in the error u.
What creates spatially correlated errors? Unmeasured influences that are similar in nearby areas:







Source
Why it is spatial




Air pollution
Varies smoothly across neighbouring areas but is incompletely measured


Healthcare access
Catchment areas and service environments cross administrative boundaries


Built environment
Unmeasured features of nearby areas resemble one another


SES / context
Area-level social conditions are rarely captured by one covariate



SEM can be viewed as modelling residual spatial structure that X did not explain.

“ρ and λ are the same thing in different models.” Both measure spatial dependence, but in different places. ρ links outcomes (and so changes how β is interpreted, through feedback). λ links errors (β keeps its usual meaning; the dependence mainly affects efficiency and standard errors). Also note: ρ in SAR is unrelated to the ρ mixing parameter in BYM2 (Session 4), which shares only the letter.


On the exam, be able to say: SEM: y = Xβ + u, u = λWu + ε. λ measures spatial dependence in the unexplained part. β is read as in OLS (no spillovers).

In short. Both models handle clustered residuals, but tell different stories: contagion between outcomes (SAR) or a shared hidden cause (SEM). The data alone rarely decide; the mechanism should.
Think of it as: Contagion vs shared weather.

Observed symptom: OLS residuals are spatially autocorrelated. Residual autocorrelation alone does not tell you which story is true.

  An increase in an area’s outcome raises its neighbours’ outcomes

  Sixty percent of the variation in the outcome is caused by geography
  λ describes dependence in the error process: the residual (unexplained) variation is spatially correlated. Outcome-to-outcome effects and impacts belong to SAR. λ is not a share of variance explained or caused by space.

title: Session 3 — Introduction to Spatial Regression
section: 3.9 A practical workflow and residual Moran’s I
text:
3.9 A practical workflow and residual Moran’s I

In short. Fit OLS, check whether the residuals cluster, think about why, compare spatial models, then interpret carefully.






flowchart LR
  A["1 · Fit OLS<br/>scientific model<br/>and covariates"] --> B["2 · Check residuals<br/>map them; test residual<br/>Moran's I"]
  B --> C["3 · Ask why<br/>what mechanism could<br/>create the dependence?"]
  C --> D["4 · Compare models<br/>SAR / SEM + diagnostics;<br/>check residuals again"]
  D --> E["5 · Interpret carefully<br/>impacts for SAR; no causal<br/>language without causal design"]


 Workflow: each arrow means “then”. Not causal. From OLS to spatial regression (slide 19). 



Diagnostics support reasoning; they do not replace it.
Residual Moran’s I asks: after fitting the model, is there evidence of remaining spatial autocorrelation? If it is significant:

something spatial remains unexplained;
it does not tell SAR from SEM by itself;
it can also reflect other misspecification or heterogeneity.

An important diagnostic goal for the spatial model: substantially reduce unexplained spatial structure (residual Moran’s I near zero after fitting SAR or SEM).

On the exam, be able to say: Residual Moran’s I detects remaining spatial structure but does not distinguish SAR from SEM, and can reflect misspecification. Diagnostics support reasoning; they do not replace it.

title: Session 3 — Introduction to Spatial Regression
section: 3.10 Lagrange multiplier (LM) tests
text:
3.10 Lagrange multiplier (LM) tests

In short. LM tests ask whether a lag term or an error term would improve the OLS model. The robust versions help when both look significant.

LM tests start from the OLS fit and ask whether adding a spatial component is supported:







Test
Question




LM-lag
Is adding a spatially lagged outcome (ρWy) supported?


LM-error
Is spatial dependence in the errors (λ) supported?


Robust LM-lag / robust LM-error
Each test made robust to the presence of the other kind of dependence. Useful when both simple LM tests are significant



A common reading: if only one simple test is significant, consider that model; if both are, look at the robust versions and see which remains clearly significant.
For this course (slide 21): know what the tests are asking. Do not memorise formulas, and do not treat p-values as the scientific mechanism. Model choice should combine theory, diagnostics and interpretability. The tests are “useful, but not a magic decision tree”.






TipWatch: Luc Anselin’s lecture on this






▶ Specification Tests: Moran’s I on residuals, LM-lag and LM-error
▶ Robust Tests: the robust LM tests

Optional, from the Canvas post. Luc Anselin’s lecture series Applied Spatial Regression Analysis goes beyond STA530 in places.




On the exam, be able to say: LM-lag tests for a spatially lagged outcome, LM-error for spatially dependent errors; robust versions are used when both are significant. Know what they ask; combine with theory.

title: Session 3 — Introduction to Spatial Regression
section: 3.11 Which model story fits better?
text:
3.11 Which model story fits better?

In short. Pick the model whose story matches the process: a shared, poorly measured environment → SEM; an outcome that spreads → SAR.

The slide’s two scenarios:








Scenario
Natural starting model
Why




A. Neighbouring municipalities share an incompletely measured air-quality environment
SEM
The dependence comes from an omitted, spatially smooth exposure: correlated errors


B. An infectious outcome diffuses through movement between connected municipalities
SAR may be plausible
Outcomes in one area directly affect outcomes in connected areas



Real analyses can be less clean. The point is to articulate the assumed process.

  Spatial lag (SAR), because uptake itself spreads between areas
  Spatial error (SEM), because uptake is shaped by unmeasured factors
  OLS, because spatial dependence never affects the estimated β
  A model with no W, since diffusion is not a geographic process
  Social diffusion of behaviour is an outcome-to-outcome process, which is what ρWy represents. With SAR, remember to report direct and indirect (spillover) impacts instead of β alone.


On the exam, be able to say: Shared incompletely measured air quality → SEM; infectious diffusion between connected areas → SAR. The point is to state the assumed process.

section: 3.12 Deliberately not covered in STA530

3.12 Deliberately not covered in STA530

In short. Estimation methods and more advanced spatial models are outside the course.

title: Session 3 — Introduction to Spatial Regression
section: 3.13 Take-home messages and key questions
text:
3.13 Take-home messages and key questions

Check geography after regression. Spatial structure can remain after covariate adjustment.
SAR and SEM encode different mechanisms: outcome feedback versus spatially correlated errors.
SAR changes interpretation: direct and indirect impacts matter because of feedback.
Diagnostics are evidence, not answers: use residual checks and tests together with scientific reasoning.







NoteWhy is β in a SAR model not the full effect of x?





Because y appears on both sides. A change in x in one area changes y there, which changes neighbours’ y through ρW, which feeds back. The total effect is captured by (I − ρW)⁻¹β; with row-standardized W the total impact is β/(1 − ρ), larger than β when ρ > 0.









NoteResidual Moran’s I is significant. Why can you not conclude that SAR is the right model?





Because both SAR (outcome dependence) and SEM (error dependence) produce autocorrelated OLS residuals, and so can misspecification or spatial heterogeneity. The diagnostic says something spatial is unexplained, not which mechanism. Theory, LM tests and interpretability have to be combined.









NoteWhat does ρ represent in SAR, and λ in SEM?





ρ is the strength of dependence between an area’s outcome and its neighbours’ outcomes (through Wy). λ is the strength of spatial dependence in the error process: how spatially structured the unexplained part is.









NoteWhy might OLS standard errors be wrong with positively autocorrelated residuals?





OLS treats every area as an independent piece of information. If neighbouring residuals are alike, the effective amount of information is smaller than n, so the true sampling variability of β̂ is larger than OLS reports: standard errors too small, confidence intervals too narrow, p-values too small.

title: Session 5 — Computer Lab
text:
Session 5 was the computer lab. It started by finishing the remaining Bayesian disease-mapping lecture material (Session 4) and then brought the main methods of the course together on one dataset: real geography and socioeconomic data from Västra Götaland with simulated health outcomes.
This page does not reproduce the lab or its solutions (the site is public). It shows what each part of the lab is for and how to read its results, using made-up data. That is also what the written exam asks for: concepts and interpretation, not code.

title: Session 5 — Computer Lab
section: 5.1 The lab as one workflow
text:
5.1 The lab as one workflow

In short. The three parts of the lab are three questions about the same map: is there a spatial pattern? (ESDA), can covariates explain it, and what about the dependence that remains? (spatial regression), what is each area’s underlying risk, and how sure are we? (Bayesian disease mapping).






flowchart LR
  A["Part I · ESDA (GeoDa)<br/>weights, raw vs smoothed rates,<br/>Moran's I, LISA"] --> B["Part II · Spatial regression (R)<br/>OLS → residual Moran's I<br/>→ SAR or SEM"]
  B --> C["Part III · Bayesian disease mapping (R-INLA)<br/>BYM2 → posterior RR<br/>→ exceedance probabilities"]


 Workflow: each arrow means “then”. Not causal. The three parts of the computer lab. 











Part
Question
Main output to interpret




I · ESDA
Is the outcome spatially clustered, and where?
Rate maps, Moran’s I with permutation p-value, LISA cluster map


II · Spatial regression
How is the outcome associated with area characteristics, and is there dependence left over?
β from OLS, SAR and SEM; residual Moran’s I; ρ or λ


III · Bayesian disease mapping
What is the underlying relative risk in each area, accounting for small numbers?
Posterior RR map, credible intervals, P(RR > 1) map




On the exam, be able to say: A typical spatial analysis explores patterns first (maps, Moran’s I, LISA), then models associations while handling dependence (OLS → SAR/SEM), and estimates small-area risks with uncertainty (BYM2: posterior RR, credible intervals, exceedance probabilities).

title: Session 5 — Computer Lab
section: 5.2 Part I: exploring patterns with maps and autocorrelation
text:
5.2 Part I: exploring patterns with maps and autocorrelation

In short. Before modelling: define neighbours, compare raw and smoothed rates, test the whole map with Moran’s I, and find where the clusters are with LISA.

The order of the steps matters, and each has its own interpretation:



Step
What to look at
How to read it




1 · Spatial weights
Contiguity (queen/rook) or distance; connectivity histogram
Areas with 0 neighbours (islands) need attention; the choice of W affects everything after (2.10)


2 · Raw vs smoothed rates
A map of crude rates next to an Empirical Bayes smoothed map
Extreme values that disappear after smoothing were probably small-population noise (2.6)


3 · Global Moran’s I
I, its expected value −1/(n−1), and the permutation p-value
I > 0 and small p: similar values cluster more than under spatial randomness (2.11)


4 · LISA
Significance map and cluster map (HH, LL, HL, LH)
Where the hot and cold spots and the outliers are; many local tests, so be careful with p-values (2.13)




Common confusion: “a significant global Moran’s I tells you where the clusters are.” No: global Moran’s I is one number for the whole map. Where the clusters are is the question LISA answers.


On the exam, be able to say: Define W, compare raw and smoothed rates (unstable small areas), test for global clustering with Moran’s I (permutation inference), and locate clusters and outliers with LISA (HH, LL, HL, LH).

title: Session 5 — Computer Lab
section: 5.3 Part II: two basic ways to represent spatial dependence
text:
5.3 Part II: two basic ways to represent spatial dependence

In short. SAR: dependence enters through the outcome, an area’s outcome is related to its neighbours’ outcomes. SEM: dependence enters through the error, unmeasured influences are spatially correlated. The same observed clustering can come from very different substantive stories.

This recap was shown in the lab (lecture notes):







Spatial lag model · SAR
Spatial error model · SEM




Dependence enters through the outcome
Dependence enters through the error process


An area’s outcome is related to outcomes in neighbouring areas
Unmeasured influences are spatially correlated


Consider: interaction, diffusion, feedback
Consider: omitted spatially patterned determinants



What is Wy? (lecture notes)

W defines who is a neighbour, and how much they count.
y is the outcome in every area.
Wy is a spatially lagged outcome: a weighted summary of the neighbours’ y. With a row-standardized W it is the average of the neighbours’ values (3.3).


Worked example. Area 1 has three neighbours with rates 12, 15 and 18; row-standardized weights are 1/3 each. (Wy)₁ = (12 + 15 + 18)/3 = 15. If area 1’s own rate is 20, it is higher than its neighbourhood average: a candidate HL outlier in LISA terms.


On the exam, be able to say: SAR puts dependence in the outcome (y depends on Wy: interaction, diffusion, feedback); SEM puts it in the error (spatially patterned omitted variables). Wy is the weighted average of the neighbours’ outcomes. The same clustering can fit either story, so choose by mechanism.

title: Session 5 — Computer Lab
section: 5.4 Reading the SAR and SEM parameters
text:
5.4 Reading the SAR and SEM parameters

In short. In SAR, ρ says how strongly outcomes are linked through W; in SEM, λ says how strongly the unobserved error is spatially structured. β means something slightly different in each.

Spatial lag model (SAR):
\[
y = \rho W y + X\beta + \varepsilon
\]



Symbol
Meaning (lab recap)




ρ · spatial dependence
How strongly outcomes are linked through W


β · covariates
Association with X, conditional on the spatial process. Not the full effect: report direct, indirect and total impacts (3.5)


ε · remaining noise
The remaining error, assumed independent



The key idea: y in one area is jointly determined with y in neighbouring areas.
Spatial error model (SEM):
\[
y = X\beta + u, \qquad u = \lambda W u + \varepsilon
\]







Symbol
Meaning (lab recap)




λ · error dependence
How strongly the unobserved error process is spatially structured


β · covariates
Regression associations after accounting for correlated errors; interpreted as in OLS


ε · innovation
The remaining independent error



Here, neighbouring y values are not directly placed on the right-hand side.
What to compare across OLS, SAR and SEM (concepts, made-up reasoning):

Residual Moran’s I. Clearly positive after OLS, close to zero after a well-specified SAR or SEM: the dependence has been modelled.
Coefficients. In SEM, β is usually close to OLS, but with more honest (typically larger) standard errors. In SAR, β is not comparable to OLS directly; compare total impacts.
Fit. Log-likelihood or AIC can compare the models, and LM tests (3.10) point toward lag or error. The mechanism still decides the interpretation (3.11).


On the exam, be able to say: ρ (SAR) measures how strongly outcomes are linked through W; λ (SEM) measures how spatially structured the unobserved errors are. In SAR, β is conditional on the spatial process and impacts must be reported; in SEM, β is read as in OLS, with corrected standard errors.

title: Session 5 — Computer Lab
section: 5.5 Part III: why Bayesian smoothing for small areas
text:
5.5 Part III: why Bayesian smoothing for small areas

In short. Crude SMRs in areas with few expected cases jump around by chance, so the most extreme areas on the map are often the smallest. BYM2 borrows strength from all areas and from neighbours, so the map shows risk, not noise, and every area gets an uncertainty.

Comparing the crude SMR map with the posterior relative risk map is the central exercise of Part III (and of mini-project group 2, 8.3). What to expect:

Extremes shrink, most in areas with small expected counts (4.6).
Large areas barely change: their data dominate the prior.
The ranking changes: an area that was “worst” on the crude map may be ordinary after smoothing; an area with a moderate but precise excess may now stand out.
The spatial pattern becomes clearer: the structured effect pulls areas toward their neighbours (4.9).


On the exam, be able to say: Crude SMRs from small expected counts are unstable and dominate the extremes of the map. Bayesian smoothing (BYM2) borrows strength from all areas and neighbours, shrinking unreliable estimates most, and gives each area a posterior distribution with uncertainty.

title: Session 5 — Computer Lab
section: 5.6 Reading posterior RR and exceedance probabilities: risk classification
text:
5.6 Reading posterior RR and exceedance probabilities: risk classification

In short. Map two things: the posterior relative risk (how high) and the exceedance probability P(RR > 1) (how sure). A common rule classifies an area as elevated only when P(RR > 1) is high, for example above 0.8, and as low when it is below 0.2.

The exceedance probability turns each area’s posterior into one number for evidence (4.16). To classify areas, a threshold is needed. Richardson et al. (2004) (not on the course slides) recommend flagging an area as elevated when P(RR > 1) > 0.8; the symmetric cut-off 0.2 is often used for the lower end:



P(RR > 1)
Classification




> 0.8
Evidence of elevated risk


0.2 – 0.8
Uncertain: the data cannot tell


< 0.2
Evidence of lower risk



Richardson et al. showed by simulation that with the 0.8 rule, false alarms are rare, but real excesses of moderate size (RR around 1.5) in areas with small expected counts are often missed: smoothing makes the method conservative. Thresholds are choices; report the one you used and why.








Figure 1: Simulated posterior summaries for 100 areas. Left: posterior mean RR against expected count. Right: the same areas classified by exceedance probability with the 0.8 / 0.2 rule. Areas with small expected counts are shrunk toward 1 and mostly stay ‘uncertain’, whatever their crude SMR; the ‘elevated’ and ‘lower’ classes are reached mainly by areas with larger expected counts, some with only a modest RR.









Common confusion: “P(RR > 1) = 0.9 means the risk is 90% higher.” No: it is the posterior probability that the area’s relative risk exceeds 1, i.e. how sure we are that there is some excess. The size of the excess is read from the posterior RR and its credible interval.


On the exam, be able to say: The posterior RR shows how high the risk is; P(RR > 1) shows how sure we are that it exceeds 1. Areas can be classified with thresholds such as > 0.8 (elevated) and < 0.2 (lower); the rule is conservative and may miss moderate excesses in small areas.

title: Session 5 — Computer Lab
section: 5.7 The lab data: real geography, simulated outcomes
text:
5.7 The lab data: real geography, simulated outcomes

In short. The lab used real borders and socioeconomic data from Västra Götaland, but simulated health outcomes. The results teach methods; they say nothing about real disease patterns in the region.


GeoPackage (.gpkg) is a single-file format that holds geometry, attributes and the coordinate reference system together. Compare the shapefile, which needs several files in the same folder (.shp geometry, .dbf attributes, .shx index, .prj projection; 1.2).
Simulated outcomes are common in teaching: the instructor knows the true risk surface, so you can check whether a method recovers it. The same idea is used in the figures of this app.
The mini-project datasets (A–D) follow the same principle (Session 8).


On the exam, be able to say: A GeoPackage stores geometry, attributes and CRS in one file, unlike the multi-file shapefile. Simulated outcomes on real geography let you test whether a method recovers a known pattern, but cannot be interpreted as real disease patterns.

title: Session 7 — Guest Lecture: Equity in Cancer Detection
text: A guest lecture by Ulf Strömberg (University of Gothenburg; Professor of Epidemiologic Methods for over 20 years; leader of the Forte-funded GeoTIME programme, Geomapping for Targeted Interventions and Methods for Evaluation). It shows the methods of the course applied to a real public health question: geographic and socioeconomic inequalities in how and when cancer is detected in Sweden.

title: Session 7 — Guest Lecture: Equity in Cancer Detection
section: 7.1 Identify: which outcomes show inequality in cancer detection?
text:
7.1 Identify: which outcomes show inequality in cancer detection?

In short. The Canvas post names three outcomes whose geography can reveal inequity: cancer incidence, stage at diagnosis and screening participation. Each needs its own likelihood and denominator.




Outcome
What a geographic pattern can mean
Data structure → likelihood (4.2)




Incidence
Differences in risk factors, or in how much is detected
New cases over person-time or vs expected (age-standardized) → Poisson


Stage at diagnosis
Late detection: barriers to care, low awareness, low screening uptake
Advanced-stage cases among all diagnosed cases → Binomial


Screening participation
Unequal use of a free, organised programme
Participants among those invited → Binomial



A key point for interpretation: higher incidence is not always worse. Where more people are screened, more early cancers are found, so incidence can be higher in areas with better detection. Stage at diagnosis and participation are closer measures of equity in detection.

On the exam, be able to say: Inequity in cancer detection can be studied through incidence, stage at diagnosis and screening participation. Stage and participation are proportions (Binomial); incidence is a rate or an observed-vs-expected count (Poisson). Higher incidence can reflect better detection.

title: Session 7 — Guest Lecture: Equity in Cancer Detection
section: 7.2 Small-area data: geographic and socioeconomic inequalities together
text:
7.2 Small-area data: geographic and socioeconomic inequalities together

In short. Small-area data (for example DeSO, 1.4) can show where detection is worse and whether that follows socioeconomic gradients. The course’s small-area issues all apply.


Small numbers. Late-stage cancers per small area are few, so crude proportions are unstable; smoothing (2.6, 4.12) and exceedance probabilities (5.6) separate signal from noise.
Area-level socioeconomic data (income, education, country of birth) can be added as covariates or summarized with an index (6.17).
Ecological fallacy (1.11): an area-level association between deprivation and low participation does not show that the deprived individuals are the ones not participating.
MAUP (1.10): the inequality found can depend on the size and borders of the areas.


On the exam, be able to say: Small-area data can link geographic and socioeconomic inequalities in cancer detection, but bring the familiar problems: unstable small counts (use smoothing and exceedance probabilities), the ecological fallacy, and the MAUP.

title: Session 7 — Guest Lecture: Equity in Cancer Detection
section: 7.3 Inform and evaluate: geographically targeted interventions
text:
7.3 Inform and evaluate: geographically targeted interventions

In short. Maps can target an intervention (for example extra screening invitations or outreach in areas with low participation). Whether it worked is a causal question: it needs the designs and cautions from Session 6.

The GeoTIME name says it: geomapping for targeted interventions and methods for evaluation.



Step
Course tools
Caution




Target: choose areas
Disease mapping, exceedance probabilities, LISA hot spots
Use posterior probabilities, not crude extremes, so random noise does not decide where resources go


Intervene

Targeted areas were chosen because they were worse: spatially structured confounding (6.23) and regression to the mean


Evaluate
Difference-in-differences, matching, comparison with untargeted areas (6.25)
Parallel trends; spillover to neighbouring areas (6.27)



Regression to the mean (not on the slides): an area selected for an extreme value in one period tends to be less extreme in the next, even without intervention. A before–after comparison in the targeted areas alone would mistake this for an effect; a control group is needed.

On the exam, be able to say: Disease mapping can identify areas for targeted interventions (using posterior risks and exceedance probabilities), but evaluating the intervention is a causal question: the targeted areas were selected for being worse, so a design with comparable controls (for example DiD) is needed, with attention to spillovers and regression to the mean.
